articles.title: Artificial Intelligence, Critical Minerals, and the Financial Abandonment of American Manufacturing - InvestorNews
articles.summary: Artificial Intelligence, Critical Minerals, and the Financial Abandonment of American Manufacturing  InvestorNews
articles.full_text:
Why can American financial markets mobilize hundreds of billions of dollars annually for artificial intelligence, a technology whose ultimate profitability remains uncertain, while struggling to finance the reconstruction of industrial capabilities whose necessity is already clear?
I believe that this question goes to the heart of America’s critical minerals crisis. It also exposes a fundamental weakness in the financial system that has come to dominate American industrial policy, corporate management, and capital allocation.
Wall Street has discovered artificial intelligence, and the capital being committed to its development is extraordinary. Reuters reported on October 7, 2026, that the world’s largest technology companies’ combined capital spending plans had risen to more than $730 billion for the year. In June, Morgan Stanley projected that global AI-related debt issuance could approach $570 billion in 2026. These figures measure different aspects of financing and spending, so you can’t add them together, but they illustrate the extraordinary scale of the financial commitment to developing artificial intelligence.
Meanwhile, the International Energy Agency reported in its 2026 Global Critical Minerals Outlook that global investment in critical minerals actually declined by 9% in 2025, ending several years of growth. The same report noted that public financing commitments in advanced economies had reached approximately $65 billion, more than four times the 2023 level. Even so, this figure reflects commitments rather than actual disbursements, and it covers a broad range of critical mineral projects rather than just the processing and manufacturing capabilities I regard as the most important industrial bottlenecks.
The contrast is striking. Financial markets are prepared to finance a technological revolution whose ultimate commercial structure remains uncertain, but they remain reluctant to finance the industrial infrastructure needed to sustain the physical economy on which that revolution depends.
I am not suggesting that artificial intelligence is unimportant. I believe that it will become an increasingly valuable tool in scientific research, engineering, manufacturing, and business management. My concern is that we are once again confusing the creation of financial wealth with the creation of productive industrial capability.
I have spent more than sixty years working in, managing, researching, and observing industrial manufacturing and the technologies that support it. During that time, I have watched the United States transform from the world’s preeminent industrial manufacturing economy into one increasingly dependent on other nations’ industrial output. This transformation was not inevitable. It was the foreseeable consequence of decisions made by corporate management, investors, financial institutions, and governments. Those decisions were generally justified in the name of economic efficiency, but they too often measured efficiency by returns on financial capital rather than a nation’s long-term productive capacity.
What we now call the critical minerals crisis is, in my opinion, a symptom of a much larger problem: the financial abandonment of American industrial manufacturing.
The Extraordinary Difference Between Industrial Importance and Financial Attractiveness
The International Energy Agency has offered a particularly revealing comparison. In its 2026 study of rare earth supply chains, the agency estimated that developing diversified magnet rare earth supply chains outside the dominant supplier, China, would require about $60 billion in investment over the next decade. Nearly half of this investment would go to refining, while about one-third would go to magnet manufacturing.
Consider what this means. The estimated capital required over ten years to substantially diversify the world’s rare-earth magnet supply chain is less than one-tenth of the annual capital spending now being planned by the largest technology companies.
The comparison isn’t exact because the two figures reflect different industrial activities, geographies, and time periods. But the difference in scale is so enormous that it raises a question about our financial system’s priorities.
Why is it relatively easy to mobilize hundreds of billions of dollars to build data centers, yet so difficult to finance the chemical separation plants, metal production facilities, alloy plants, and magnet factories that underpin the manufacturing of essential electrical and electronic equipment?
The answer is not that the industrial importance of these facilities is uncertain. The IEA estimates that fully implementing China’s expanded rare earth export restrictions could jeopardize as much as $6.5 trillion in annual downstream production outside China. This estimates economic activity exposed to disruption, not a prediction that $6.5 trillion will actually be lost. Nevertheless, it illustrates the extraordinary economic leverage a relatively small number of critical materials and processing capabilities can exert.
We are discussing a potential vulnerability measured in trillions of dollars, whose mitigation may require investments measured in tens of billions.
This is an astonishing imbalance between an industrial capability’s economic importance and financial markets’ willingness to provide the capital needed to establish it.
A rare earth separation plant may be essential to producing thousands of manufactured products, yet it may never offer investors the financial returns expected from a successful artificial intelligence software company. Its value to the national economy may be enormous, while its profitability as an individual enterprise may be relatively modest.
This distinction between industrial importance and financial attractiveness is the central problem that American industrial policy has failed to resolve.
Artificial Intelligence Cannot Replace Industrial Production
Artificial intelligence is fundamentally an information-processing technology. Its economic value will ultimately depend on its ability to improve productivity, reduce costs, accelerate innovation, or create products and services customers will pay for. These are legitimate objectives, and some applications will undoubtedly become enormously valuable.
But artificial intelligence does not eliminate the physical requirements of industrial civilization.
A computer cannot manufacture an electric motor without copper, steel, insulation, and, in many applications, rare earth permanent magnets. It cannot produce a semiconductor without highly purified and precisely engineered materials. It cannot construct an electrical transmission system without conductors, transformers, and the industrial facilities required to manufacture them. It cannot build a factory without machinery, nor can it replace the chemical engineering, metallurgy, process development, and manufacturing experience required to produce materials consistently at commercial scale.
Artificial intelligence may help engineers design improved chemical separation systems. It may optimize an existing metallurgical plant’s operation. It may help identify process inefficiencies and accelerate materials research. But engineers must still demonstrate the resulting improvements in physical equipment, using actual feedstocks, under conditions that can be reproduced economically in commercial production.
The expansion of artificial intelligence may increase demand for many critical materials whose supply chains are already fragile. Data centers require enormous investments in electrical generation and distribution, cooling equipment, transformers, conductors, and electronic components. Advanced semiconductors require highly specialized materials and extraordinarily sophisticated manufacturing equipment. The physical infrastructure supporting artificial intelligence is not virtual. It is an industrial system.
It is therefore ironic that the United States is prepared to invest so heavily in artificial intelligence while remaining dependent on foreign industrial systems for much of the equipment and material inputs required to support it.
We should ask ourselves whether the United States is becoming a nation that designs the future but must purchase the materials and machinery needed to build it from someone else.
The Financialization of American Industry
The decline of American manufacturing did not begin with China’s emergence as an industrial superpower. It began when American corporate management increasingly treated manufacturing as a cost center rather than the nation’s fundamental source of economic strength.
Beginning in the latter part of the twentieth century, financial performance became the dominant measure of corporate success. Companies moved manufacturing overseas when it reduced costs and improved reported margins. Companies abandoned capital-intensive businesses for those promising higher returns on invested capital. Industrial research, process development, and training skilled manufacturing workers increasingly became expenditures to minimize rather than investments in future competitiveness.
The financial markets rewarded these decisions. A corporation that closed an American factory and purchased its output from a lower-cost foreign supplier could report improved profitability. Its shareholders benefited, at least in the short term. But the national economy lost not only the factory but also the accumulated knowledge, supplier relationships, technical workforce, and manufacturing experience that had made the factory possible.
These losses were cumulative. Once a manufacturing industry disappears, its supporting industries begin to disappear with it. Eventually, even if the final product can be designed domestically, the materials, components, production equipment, and qualified personnel needed to manufacture it may no longer be available.

articles.title: More bad news for Starlink? After India, Ukraine controversies, European telcos plan to launch own satellite service - TradingView
articles.summary: More bad news for Starlink? After India, Ukraine controversies, European telcos plan to launch own satellite service  TradingView
articles.full_text:
New Delhi, Oct. 20 -- Deutsche Telekom, Orange, Telefónica and Vodafone, Europe's four largest telecom groups, are reportedly exploring the possibility of launching their own satellite mobile services to reduce dependence on suppliers outside the bloc and challenge the dominance of billionaire Elon Musk's Starlink.
The Financial Times reported on Monday (local time) that the companies had signed a letter of intent to explore a joint bid for radio spectrum that would allow them to provide "direct-to-device" satellite mobile services across Europe. The move could further escalate transatlantic tensions over communications technology.
The development comes as Musk's Starlink faces controversies in countries ranging from Ukraine to India.
The European Commission proposed in May that spectrum used for direct smartphone-to-satellite connections be reserved for European operators. Two US companies, Viasat and EchoStar, currently use the 2 GHz band, but their licences are due to expire next year.
The initiative, which has been applauded privately, would see the companies build ground-based facilities, including base stations, to support satellite connections. However, instead of developing their own satellite constellation, the companies might collaborate with an existing provider, which has yet to be selected.
Selecting a provider could pose additional challenges, since most satellite constellations are operated by US or Chinese companies. While French satellite operator Eutelsat has developed a large-scale constellation, it remains far behind Starlink, which has over 11,000 satellites in orbit.
The proposal has heightened tensions between the US and Europe. The US ambassador to the European Union, Andrew Puzder, told the Financial Times that European companies could face "devastating" retaliation unless the bloc revised the plan, which he said would discriminate against American firms such as Starlink.
When asked whether companies in Europe should fear retaliation, Puzder said they "should be wary that it could happen and it would be very devastating for those companies", given the size of the US market.
The bloc's plan to counter Starlink's dominance in the region has drawn fierce criticism from SpaceX, which warned that the satellite programme could weaken connectivity in Ukraine. Starlink has been crucial to both civilian and military communications there since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.
Starlink connectivity in Ukraine was restricted last week following warnings from SpaceX and the US ambassador, although no direct link has been confirmed. Both US President Donald Trump and SpaceX founder Elon Musk denied responsibility for the restrictions.
On 17 October, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said speed restrictions on Starshield, the military version of Starlink's satellite service, remained in place and hindered Kyiv's ability to intercept Russian drones. His remarks came days after he first raised concerns about the restrictions.
In an online group chat with reporters at the European Union summit, Zelenskyy said, "Unfortunately, we can't use Starlink or Starshield technology on our territory today to shoot down jet-powered Shaheds." He added, "They fly, and we can stop them with aircraft and other air defense, but we don't use Starlink for that, unfortunately. God willing, this will be restored."
Denying responsibility, Musk said, "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS." Soon after, the US president said, "Well, I don't know if it was anybody because it wasn't me, and I don't think it was Elon."
Beyond Europe and Ukraine, Starlink has also faced controversy over its planned operations in India.
Earlier this month, SpaceX founder Musk escalated his criticism of Reliance Industries chairman Mukesh Ambani over delays to Starlink's launch in India. After initially blaming unnamed "oligarchs" for blocking its entry, Musk asked on 8 October, "Is Ambani the real boss of India?" The following day, he addressed Ambani as "Prime Minister Ambani" in another post questioning whether Starlink would be allowed to compete.
The Ministry of Communications rejected allegations of discrimination, saying Starlink, Bharti-backed Eutelsat OneWeb and Jio Satellite Communications had received licences but were undergoing security assessments. It said all three were at broadly the same regulatory stage and could seek spectrum assignment after completing those checks.

articles.summary: GTA 6 Platform Poll: 36% of DF Viewers to Play on PS5 Pro after 30,000 Votes  Digital FoundryGrand Theft Auto VI Launch Trailer  Rockstar GamesYou Can Watch the Newest ‘GTA VI’ Trailer One Month Before the Game’s Release  Car and DriverJustice Composed the Score for Grand Theft Auto VI  Pitchfork'GTA 6' is almost here, 13 years after 'GTA 5'. articles.full_text:
Yesterday we polled the Digital Foundry viewership on YouTube to see where Grand Theft Auto 6 players would actually play the game when it's released worldwide on November 19th. The results are surprising - after 30,000 votes, nearly 80 percent of respondents have answered that they will play on PS5 or PS5 Pro, with a nearly even split between the PS5 Pro and base PS5.
Given that the base console is significantly more affordable - and more available! - I'd have expected to see a much larger share for the base system than 43 percent to 36 percent, though I expect the Digital Foundry audience has a higher proportion of gaming enthusiasts willing to spend more on better hardware than the general population.
With nearly four-fifths of respondents citing a PlayStation console, that means just over 20 percent are expecting to play on Xbox, with the vast majority here on Xbox Series X rather than Xbox Series S. Of the 30,000 respondents, only four percent are on Xbox Series S, versus 17 percent of respondents on Series X.
When are you playing GTA 6? (4,064 votes)
- The second it unlocks on release day
- The day after it's released, I'm excited but not in a mad rush
- At some point in the future, on console
- When it comes to PC
- I'm not interested in GTA 6
The poll also saw 1.8 thousand comments, with the vast majority of these stating that they either weren't interested in the game or they were planning to play on PC - either through an official port or a community recompilation. Rockstar has yet to even announce a PC version, but historically the company has tended to release PC follow-ups within a year or two of games debuting on consoles.
It's been rumoured that the PC version for GTA 6 is coming sooner than usual - perhaps as early as the first quarter of 2027 - but there doesn't appear to be much basis for this reporting as yet. Given the extremely rapid pace of AI-accelerated game ports, decompilations and recompilations, a quicker official PC port would seem logical, but it's a complicated multi-factor decision for Rockstar to make.

articles.title: Robotic therapy for stroke patients
articles.summary: Strokes leave 5 million people with long-term impairments each year, and a growing shortage of physical therapists makes it hard for them to get the care they need. articles.full_text:
Strokes leave 5 million people with long-term impairments each year, and a growing shortage of physical therapists makes it hard for them to get the care they need. A new approach tries to solve that problem by combining artificial intelligence and human therapy. 



Johannes Lachner, a former MIT postdoc who is now an assistant professor at Purdue University, and Noah Geiger, a former visiting student at MIT, developed a robotic system that uses generative AI and real-time force feedback to learn from real therapists. Drawing on what it’s learned, it gives patients just the right amount of assistance during physical rehabilitation exercises like reaching, lifting their arms, and performing tasks of daily living.



The goal is “not to replace therapists, but to extend their reach,” Lachner says. 









“Initial robotic experiments have already demonstrated the feasibility of this approach,” he reports. “The next phase of the project aims to develop therapist-specific models and evaluate them in a long-term clinical study with the same patients who previously received manual therapy.” Beyond that, he envisions possible applications in contact-rich industrial settings or collaborative workspaces.

articles.title: ByteDance, Alibaba and Tencent Place $35 Billion Nvidia AI Chip Orders as China Faces GPU Shortage - InfotechLead
articles.summary: ByteDance, Alibaba and Tencent Place $35 Billion Nvidia AI Chip Orders as China Faces GPU Shortage  InfotechLead
articles.full_text:
The three Chinese technology companies have collectively ordered more than 3 million Nvidia RTX PRO 5500 GPUs, priced at approximately $11,400 each. However, Nvidia has warned customers that it may be unable to fulfill most of these orders because demand substantially exceeds its planned manufacturing capacity.
Total Chinese orders for the RTX PRO 5500 have reportedly surpassed 6 million units, potentially representing more than $68 billion in hardware at the indicated unit price. These figures represent reported order demand rather than confirmed shipments or recognized revenue.
Nvidia AI Chip Orders: Key Figures for 2026–2027
| Indicator | Reported figures | 
| ByteDance, Alibaba and Tencent orders | More than $35 billion | 
| Combined orders from three companies | More than 3 million GPUs | 
| Total Chinese customer orders | More than 6 million GPUs | 
| Nvidia RTX PRO 5500 unit price | Approximately $11,400 | 
| Potential value of all Chinese orders | More than $68 billion | 
| Maximum indicated global production in 2027 | 3 million GPUs | 
| Potential fulfillment communicated to partners | 5–10% of requested quantities | 
| Initial product samples | December 2026 | 
| Expected commercial deliveries | Q1 2027 | 
The figures illustrate a significant mismatch between China’s demand for AI computing capacity and Nvidia’s expected GPU supply.
Why ByteDance, Alibaba and Tencent Are Buying Nvidia RTX PRO 5500 GPUs
Chinese technology companies are accelerating investments in AI infrastructure to support large language models, cloud computing, enterprise AI applications and consumer-facing AI services.
ByteDance, the parent company of TikTok and Douyin, operates large digital platforms requiring extensive computing infrastructure. Its AI initiatives include recommendation systems, content generation and conversational AI applications.
Alibaba is expanding its AI capabilities through Alibaba Cloud and the Qwen family of AI models. These services require substantial computing resources to support enterprise customers, developers and AI applications.
Tencent operates major cloud, gaming, social networking and digital services businesses. Its AI investments support enterprise cloud services, digital content, advertising and AI-enabled applications.
The RTX PRO 5500 orders reflect demand for hardware capable of supporting AI inference, the process of running trained AI models to generate responses, predictions and other outputs.
Unlike large-scale AI training, inference workloads can often operate on less powerful processors, depending on model size, latency requirements and deployment architecture.
This makes workstation-class GPUs a potential alternative for Chinese companies unable to obtain Nvidia’s most advanced data-center accelerators.
The reported orders have not been independently confirmed by the three buyers, and individual company order values have not been disclosed.
US Export Restrictions Increase Demand for Nvidia’s Alternative AI Chips
US semiconductor export restrictions have significantly affected the availability of advanced Nvidia AI processors in China.
Nvidia’s Blackwell-based B300 data-center processors cannot be supplied to Chinese buyers under current US export controls, while shipments of Hopper-based H200 processors require individual regulatory review and licensing.
The RTX PRO 5500 is designed primarily for professional workstations rather than large AI data-center clusters.
However, its computing capabilities make it attractive for selected AI inference workloads.
| Nvidia GPU | Primary application | China market situation | 
| B300 | Advanced AI training and inference | Sales prohibited under current restrictions | 
| H200 | AI training and inference | Case-by-case export approval | 
| RTX PRO 5500 | Workstations and AI inference | Available under current restrictions | 
| RTX 6000D | Export-compliant AI workloads | Discontinued; resale prices have increased | 
The RTX PRO 5500 provides lower performance than Nvidia’s most advanced data-center chips, but its relative accessibility has become a significant purchasing consideration.
For Chinese AI developers, obtaining adequate computing capacity can be more important than securing the highest-performing accelerator.
Nvidia Could Supply Only 5–10% of Requested GPU Orders
Nvidia’s biggest challenge is meeting the unprecedented demand for its RTX PRO 5500 graphics cards.
The company has reportedly informed partners that deliveries could amount to only 5–10 percent of requested quantities.
At the same time, Nvidia has indicated that global RTX PRO 5500 production may not exceed 3 million units during 2027.
This is particularly significant because Chinese customer orders alone have surpassed 6 million units.
If Nvidia produces 3 million cards globally, that output would represent less than half of the reported Chinese order volume, even before considering demand from other markets.
The 5–10 percent fulfillment guidance is a separate indication of potential customer allocations and should not be interpreted as a confirmed production forecast.
Nvidia’s ability to increase manufacturing capacity will depend partly on production priorities at Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC).
Nvidia Rubin AI Platform Competes for TSMC Manufacturing Capacity
Nvidia is preparing to allocate substantial semiconductor manufacturing resources to Rubin, its next-generation AI computing platform.
Rubin is intended to support increasingly demanding AI training and inference workloads in large data centers.
Beginning in 2027, Nvidia is expected to prioritize manufacturing capacity at TSMC for Rubin and other advanced AI processors.
This could limit production flexibility for workstation-oriented products such as the RTX PRO 5500.
The allocation decision reflects the competing demands of Nvidia’s global AI customers.
Major cloud providers and AI infrastructure operators require advanced processors for large computing clusters, while Chinese technology companies are seeking alternative GPUs that comply with export restrictions.
Nvidia must balance these requirements against semiconductor manufacturing capacity, product profitability and regulatory constraints.
Nvidia RTX 6000D Prices Double as Chinese AI Chip Supply Tightens
China’s semiconductor shortage has also changed demand for previously unpopular Nvidia products.
Nvidia introduced the RTX 6000D in 2025 as a reduced-performance GPU designed to comply with US export restrictions.
Chinese technology companies initially showed limited interest because they considered its price unattractive relative to computing performance.
Some buyers expected Washington to eventually relax restrictions on more advanced Nvidia processors.
However, continuing export controls and shortages of AI computing capacity have changed purchasing decisions.
The RTX 6000D has since been discontinued, and its market price in China has reportedly more than doubled.
This illustrates how limited GPU availability can increase the commercial value of older or lower-performance processors.
The RTX PRO 5500 has emerged as another option because its performance characteristics are similar to those of the RTX 6000D.
Huawei and Chinese AI Chipmakers Gain Opportunities
US export restrictions have also created opportunities for domestic semiconductor suppliers.
Huawei has strengthened its position in China’s AI processor market as local technology companies seek alternatives to Nvidia.
China is encouraging greater adoption of domestically developed semiconductor technologies to reduce dependence on foreign suppliers.
However, Chinese chip manufacturers continue to face challenges involving advanced semiconductor fabrication, manufacturing equipment, software compatibility and ecosystem development.
Nvidia retains advantages through its GPU computing architecture and established software ecosystem, although domestic competitors are investing to reduce these gaps.
The reported $35 billion orders demonstrate that Chinese technology companies continue to value Nvidia processors even while increasing investments in domestic alternatives.
Tansun Technology Orders 20,000 Nvidia RTX PRO 5500 GPUs
Demand extends beyond China’s three largest technology companies.
Shenzhen-listed Tansun Technology disclosed in an October 13, 2026 filing that it had agreed to purchase 20,000 Nvidia RTX PRO 5500 graphics cards from an unidentified supplier.
At the reported price of approximately $11,400 per card, the order would have an indicative hardware value of about $228 million, although the company’s actual contracted price was not disclosed.
Tansun warned that semiconductor supply shortages, market demand and international technology restrictions could affect deliveries.
The transaction provides another example of Chinese companies seeking additional AI computing resources despite uncertain hardware availability.
What the $35 Billion Nvidia Orders Mean for AI Infrastructure Investment
The latest developments highlight three important trends in China’s AI infrastructure market.
First, demand for inference computing is expanding as technology companies deploy AI models across cloud platforms, enterprise applications and consumer services.
Second, US export controls are reshaping GPU procurement strategies. Chinese companies are purchasing workstation-class processors and other available alternatives rather than relying exclusively on high-end data-center accelerators.
Third, manufacturing capacity has become a major constraint. Nvidia’s reported inability to satisfy RTX PRO 5500 orders indicates that demand for AI hardware extends beyond its flagship products.

articles.title: Vulcan Elements and North Carolina Collaboratory Partner to Advance Rare Earth Magnet Innovation Through University of North Carolina-Chapel Hill Research - PR Newswire
articles.summary: Vulcan Elements and North Carolina Collaboratory Partner to Advance Rare Earth Magnet Innovation Through University of North Carolina-Chapel Hill Research  PR Newswire
articles.full_text:
Collaboration Pairs UNC-Chapel Hill's Computational Chemistry Expertise with Vulcan's Advanced Magnet Manufacturing to Support National Security and Economic Growth
DURHAM, N.C., Oct. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Vulcan Elements, an American rare earth magnet manufacturer, today announced a partnership with the North Carolina Collaboratory to advance the development of high-performance rare earth magnets for critical defense and commercial technology applications. The collaboration brings together Vulcan Elements and leading scientific expertise at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill (UNC-Chapel Hill), where research led by chemistry professor Yosuke Kanai, PhD, will develop a novel analytic capability using quantum-mechanical simulations to predict with significant accuracy how changes at the atomic level affect magnetic properties, ultimately setting a new standard for Vulcan's magnetic performance.
The partnership represents a convergence of two research fields that are foundational to national security and the future economy: rare earth magnets and quantum mechanics. The research will pair Kanai's more than 25 years of experience in computational materials research with Vulcan Elements' expertise in manufacturing rare earth magnets.
The Collaboratory is supporting the partnership through a $600,000 research award, helping support the application of UNC-Chapel Hill's scientific expertise to advance rare earth magnet innovation. Established by the North Carolina General Assembly in 2016, the Collaboratory works with academic experts across the state to transform research into practical applications for the benefit of North Carolina. Since its inception, the Collaboratory has managed more than $300 million in state appropriations and supported more than 800 research projects.
"This collaboration with the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill reflects Vulcan Elements' commitment to driving the next generation of magnetics innovation and fostering the American magnetics workforce," said John Maslin, Vulcan Elements' CEO. "This collaboration is a model for the kind of public-private partnerships that this nation needs: generating cutting-edge breakthrough technologies and translating them into real-world manufacturing capabilities that deliver for our economy and national security."
"Rare earth magnets are increasingly important to our national security and economy, and North Carolina has an opportunity to play a meaningful role in this growing sector," said Jeff Warren, PhD, executive director of the NC Collaboratory. "This partnership is exactly the kind of work the Collaboratory was created to support when we were established by the NC General Assembly—connecting world-class research expertise in our state with industry in order to solve real-world challenges. By bringing Dr. Kanai's computational research together with Vulcan's synthesis and manufacturing capabilities, we can help advance innovation that has implications well beyond the laboratory."
The collaboration comes as demand for rare earth magnets is rapidly growing across industries vital to national security and economic competitiveness. Rare earth magnets are required components in critical technologies from semiconductor fabrication, robotics, and automobiles to drones, satellites, and virtually every military system. For decades, the United States has been reliant on China for these magnets. Today, China produces up to 98% of the global supply. To its knowledge, Vulcan is the only rare earth magnet company in the world that is decoupled from China—down to the material, technology, software, IP, and ownership. The partnership with UNC-Chapel Hill advances this mission by bolstering a robust magnetics and manufacturing workforce. It also highlights Vulcan's commitment to innovating and leveraging advanced capabilities in order to develop leapfrog technologies and deliver the highest performance at competitive prices.
Vulcan Elements' Benson, North Carolina, manufacturing facility, currently under construction, will be the cornerstone of a domestic rare earth magnet supply chain and the largest rare earth magnet factory outside of China. The 1.1 million-square-foot facility will have an annual capacity of 10,000 metric tons of magnet production and will supply magnets for critical defense systems, semiconductor fabrication, robotics, drones, AI infrastructure, automobiles, and other strategic technologies and sectors of the American economy. The project will create 1,000 manufacturing jobs in North Carolina while reshoring an essential capability that has been controlled and weaponized by America's competitors for decades.
About Vulcan Elements
Vulcan Elements is an American rare earth magnet manufacturer driven by a core mission: to rebuild a secure, resilient rare earth magnet supply chain for America and its allies, and enable the technologies that will define the 21st century. Vulcan's world-class engineering, scientific rigor, and uncompromising work ethic are onshoring a fundamental capability to the United States and setting a new standard for advanced rare earth magnet production. The company partners across the public and private sectors to advance economic competitiveness, revitalize the industrial workforce, and strengthen national security.

Satellites in the sky, patents for a network that does not exist yet, and artificial intelligence inside everyday phone calls. These were the three bets that Akash Ambani laid out for Jio at this year's India Mobile Congress.
The 10th edition of the event was inaugurated by Prime Minister Narendra Modi on October 8 in New Delhi, under the theme ‘Scale Without Boundaries’
1
. On the sidelines, Akash Ambani, chairman of Reliance Jio Infocomm, spoke about where the company is heading next.
The first bet is in space. Akash told news agency NewsKerala
2
 that Jio is building an indigenous satellite communications stack based in India. He said Jio had already demonstrated it to the communications minister and was moving ahead on regulatory approvals, as reported by Entrepreneur India
3
. He described satellite services as an extension of Jio's broadband push, with home broadband as a main use, but did not give a launch timeline at the event, the report said.

, the company showed a proposed constellation of about 1,600 low-earth-orbit satellites and 23 ground stations across India, aimed at connecting more than 600,000 villages, including maritime and border areas. Jio itself described both numbers as part of a proposed plan, the report added.
The second bet is 6G, the next generation of mobile networks. "

NEW YORK (AP) — SpaceX reported a bigger quarterly profit than expected Tuesday as its satellite communications and artificial intelligence businesses boomed.
The company, run by Elon Musk, posted a profit for the three months through September of $4.4 billion, or 35 cents per share, reversing a year-ago loss and easily topping Wall Street's expectations. Revenue soared to $14.6 billion, up 161%.
On a conference call with analysts, Musk suggested a merger with his electric car company Tesla might be in the works, something that has been rumored for months. He said both companies formed “special committees” of independent directors to discuss the issue, though he played down the chances of an imminent deal.
“Some people out there assume that a SpaceX and Tesla merger is a certainty,” he said. “I think that would be overstating it.”
The AI business became SpaceX's largest by revenue in the third quarter, although the Starlink satellite service remains the biggest profit generator.
“They beat across all metrics and the Starlink business looks to be accelerating,” said Dan Ives, an analyst at Yorkville Ives. “This is just what (Wall) Street wanted.”
The stock rose 7.5% in after-hours trading.
Musk also told analysts that for next month's launch of its Starship rocket, SpaceX will attempt to grab both the booster and ship with mechanical arms upon return to base, a key step toward demonstrating it can reuse the massive spacecraft.
“The only way that we can extend consciousness beyond Earth on a sustained basis is with a fully reusable orbital launch vehicle,” Musk said, calling the attempt, if successful, “a massive technology milestone.”
SpaceX hopes to get Starship on a regular launch pattern in preparation for NASA's upcoming lunar missions.
The company already has huge contracts with the federal government, and House Democrats have called for investigations into those contracts and Musk’s work with the Department of Government Efficiency. Musk has spent $276 million since July in support of Republican candidates.
In a filing for its initial public offering in June, SpaceX warned that a change in control of Congress could have a “material and adverse impact on our growth and competitive position.”
Musk recently drew criticism from politicians in Washington after speeds for a military version of SpaceX's satellite communications service were slowed for Ukraine following President Donald Trump's deal to get more diesel oil from Russia amid a push to end the war. The Wall Street Journal reported Tuesday that it was Musk who ordered the slowdown, impeding Ukraine’s use of drones along the front. SpaceX did not immediately respond to an Associated Press request for comment on the Journal story.
Both Trump and Musk have denied responsibility for the slowdown.
As midterm elections near, Musk on Monday promised to give one share of SpaceX to “every kid in America” next year, though he provided no details on how the distribution would be carried out. With communities nationwide protesting the construction of large data centers and concerns about AI safety, AI companies are trying to build goodwill. Anthropic pledged to commit 5% of its shares to a new “public benefit” fund.
SpaceX shares have been under pressure over concerns that the company was spending too much on major projects to compete with rivals such as Anthropic. The company said capital expenditures totaled $19.6 billion last quarter, nearly triple the figure from a year earlier, and it forecast spending would grow to $35 billion to $40 billion in the current quarter.
Shares of SpaceX closed Tuesday at $147.79, down from a peak near $201 after its IPO, which made Musk the world’s first trillionaire at the time. But the share prices for SpaceX and Tesla have since dropped, reducing his net worth to $925 billion, according to Forbes magazine.
Tesla reports third-quarter financial results Wednesday. Last week, Tesla unveiled a new Roadster sports car that in some versions may include thrusters allowing it to briefly fly using SpaceX technology — though experts say anything usable for drivers is a long shot.

articles.full_text:
Google is making the Gemini AI assistant that’s already in millions of cars, trucks, and SUVs a lot more personal — a move that could push consumers even deeper into the company’s ecosystem of products.
The company said Tuesday it’s upgrading Gemini in vehicles with a personal intelligence feature that can draw on information from Gmail, Google Calendar, YouTube, Maps, Google Search history, and other connected Google services to understand your preferences, activities, and past experiences.
Google said it will roll out “Personal Intelligence with Gemini” to vehicles in two ways — through Android Auto, an app that runs on the user’s phone and wirelessly communicates with and projects navigation, media, and messaging to the vehicle’s infotainment system, and Google Built-in, software and services that have been directly integrated into the vehicle.
The feature will launch in Android Auto, starting today, and expand to cars with Google Built-in in the coming months.
Google initially launched Gemini last November in Android Auto. Meanwhile, Gemini’s “Personal Intelligence” feature rolled out across the U.S. in March and is now in beta in global markets.
This latest upgrade would connect the dots — as Google put it in its blog post — across users’ Google apps.
Drivers will have to opt in for Personalized Intelligence to work. Once a user does so, they should expect all sorts of cross-pollination. For instance, a driver who is navigating to the airport may be alerted that the flight on their calendar is delayed.
Google said the feature will allow users to make complex requests using natural language. Returning to that airport example, a user might ask the AI assistant for their flight gate before quickly following up with a question about whether it’s still on time. Gemini will give the user answers to both questions at the same time, the company said.
That level of emmeshing might make consumers uncomfortable, although Google says users do retain full control over their data with Personal Intelligence. The feature can be turned on or off at any time, and users can selectively choose which apps they’d like to connect, Google said.

- If the disruptions impacted whether American personnel were able to shelter amid the Russian attacks;

- What caused the speed restrictions—including policy decisions, or technical problems;
- What DoD is doing to make sure Americans remain safe—and receive adequate missile-warning info going forward.

articles.title: China’s $35B Nvidia GPU Order Tests Export Limits [2026] - shattered.io
articles.summary: China’s $35B Nvidia GPU Order Tests Export Limits [2026]  shattered.io
articles.full_text:
Three of China’s biggest technology companies have placed one of the largest chip orders in Nvidia’s history, and the size of the deal is colliding head-on with the limits of U.S. export law. Reuters reported on Tuesday, October 20, 2026, that ByteDance, Alibaba, and Tencent have ordered more than 3 million of Nvidia’s new RTX Pro 5500 graphics cards, a batch with a combined sticker price above $35 billion. The catch: Nvidia told customers and partners it cannot promise to deliver anywhere close to that volume.
The report, citing two people familiar with the matter, lands at a strange intersection of corporate ambition and government restriction. The RTX Pro 5500 exists specifically because Nvidia is barred from selling its most powerful AI accelerators to Chinese buyers. What was supposed to be a compliant workaround has instead triggered demand that may outstrip what Nvidia can physically build next year. That mismatch, more than the headline number itself, is the real story behind the $35 billion figure making the rounds across global business desks today.
What ByteDance, Alibaba, and Tencent Actually Ordered
According to Reuters, the three companies have collectively ordered more than 3 million Nvidia RTX Pro 5500 cards. The outlet pegged the price at roughly $11,400 per card, which multiplies out to the widely quoted “$35 billion” figure. Reuters described the combined total as a “collective sticker price,” language that matters a great deal here. A sticker price is not a signed contract, a wired payment, or a confirmed shipment. It is a list-value calculation based on how many units were requested and what each would cost at standard pricing.
Reuters also reported that total Chinese demand for the RTX Pro 5500, across all buyers and not just the three named firms, has topped 6 million cards. That figure alone tells you something important: ByteDance, Alibaba, and Tencent together account for roughly half of all Chinese orders for this chip, but they are far from the only buyers lining up.
None of the three companies responded to Reuters’ request for comment, and Nvidia has not issued a public statement confirming the order size, the dollar figure, or its production plans. No individual company breakdown exists either. Reuters did not disclose how much ByteDance ordered versus Alibaba or Tencent, so any claim about which buyer is driving the bulk of the demand is currently just a guess dressed up as analysis.
Why the RTX Pro 5500 Exists: Export Compliance by Design
The RTX Pro 5500 is not Nvidia’s flagship chip. It is a deliberately scaled-back product built to clear the technical thresholds that U.S. export rules impose on sales to China. Reuters characterized it as a “less powerful, export-compliant alternative” that Chinese buyers are seeking precisely because Washington has cut off their access to Nvidia’s most advanced AI accelerators.
This is not a new playbook for Nvidia. The company has spent several years iterating on chips designed specifically to sit just under whatever performance ceiling U.S. regulators set at a given moment. The H20 emerged after an earlier round of restrictions closed off higher-end parts to Chinese customers. Reports place the newer B30A in the same lineage, though the exact approval terms and technical thresholds for that chip have not been independently documented in current coverage. The RTX Pro 5500 is simply the latest entry in that sequence: a chip engineered around a rulebook rather than around raw performance.
Seoul Economic Daily, summarizing the Reuters reporting, noted that the RTX Pro 5500’s specifications are broadly comparable to Nvidia’s RTX 6000D, another product built to stay inside the compliance envelope. Beyond that comparison, detailed specs for the RTX Pro 5500, including memory capacity, core counts, and bandwidth, have not surfaced in confirmed reporting. What is confirmed is intent: these cards are reportedly aimed mainly at AI inference workloads rather than general workstation graphics, giving Chinese firms a way to keep running large-scale AI products even without access to top-tier accelerators.
The Math Behind the $35 Billion Headline
Running the numbers shows the arithmetic checks out, at least as a rough estimate. Multiply 3 million cards by $11,400 and the result is $34.2 billion, close enough to “over $35 billion” once you account for rounding or a slightly higher unit count. That consistency is reassuring in one narrow sense: nobody appears to have fabricated the headline number out of thin air.
But sticker value and actual revenue are different things, and conflating them is where a lot of the excitement around this story runs ahead of the facts. A sticker price reflects what a full, unconstrained order would cost. It says nothing about discounts, partial fulfillment, financing terms, or whether Nvidia will even accept every unit requested. Given that Nvidia reportedly cannot build enough cards to cover the order, the $35 billion figure functions more as a measure of pent-up demand than a forecast of money that will actually change hands in 2027.
| Reported Figure | Value | Source Status | 
|---|---|---|
| Combined RTX Pro 5500 cards ordered (3 firms) | More than 3 million units | Reuters, citing two sources familiar with the matter | 
| Estimated price per card | Approximately $11,400 | Reuters source estimate | 
| Implied combined sticker value | More than $35 billion | Arithmetic derived from quantity and price | 
| Total Chinese market demand for the chip | More than 6 million units | Reuters, citing sources | 
| Nvidia’s indicated 2027 global production capacity | No more than 3 million units | Reported estimate, not an Nvidia public forecast | 
| Reported potential allocation to requesting customers | As low as 5% to 10% of requested volume | Secondary coverage citing Reuters | 
Nvidia’s Production Problem: Demand Outstrips Supply
The most consequential detail in the Reuters report has nothing to do with China policy. It is a supply chain admission. Reuters reported, citing a third person familiar with the matter, that Nvidia has warned customers and partners it cannot guarantee fulfilling the RTX Pro 5500 orders because combined demand already exceeds what the company planned to produce. If Chinese buyers alone want more than 6 million cards and Nvidia’s entire global 2027 output tops out around 3 million, the math simply does not work, even before accounting for demand from customers outside China.
Secondary coverage citing the Reuters reporting put a sharper number on the shortfall, suggesting customers might receive only 5% to 10% of what they requested. If that estimate holds, the practical outcome of this story is not a $35 billion payday for Nvidia next year. It is a rationing exercise, with ByteDance, Alibaba, and Tencent competing against each other and against buyers in other markets for a production run that was already spoken for several times over before the ink dried on any purchase order.
This also raises an uncomfortable question for Nvidia’s China strategy. Building artificial scarcity into a compliant chip line might protect the company from accusations that it is flooding China with AI compute, but it also means the RTX Pro 5500 cannot realistically replace the capacity that higher-end, restricted chips would have provided. Chinese AI labs are effectively being asked to do more inference work with a chip that is both less capable and in short supply.
A Pattern Years in the Making: From H20 to RTX Pro 5500
None of this happened overnight. Washington’s restrictions on advanced AI chip sales to China have pushed Nvidia into a cycle of designing, shipping, and eventually replacing China-specific products as the rules shift underneath them. The H20 was the company’s answer to an earlier round of controls, built specifically to stay under the performance line regulators drew at the time. The B30A followed as part of that same pattern of adaptation, though current reporting does not establish a verified timeline of its approval or technical limits.
What makes the RTX Pro 5500 situation notable is scale. articles.full_text:
SpaceX pulled off a pair of launches in the span of a week while simultaneously finding itself at the center of a political tug-of-war over how its satellite services are used in Ukraine. The company's Bandwagon-5 rideshare mission lifted off with a Falcon 9, carrying 32 payloads to orbit, and the rocket's first stage came back down for a landing on the Atlantic drone ship A Shortfall of Gravitas. The flight represents a clean operational win, though it says nothing on its own about revenue or profit from the mission.
Two days earlier, on October 15, a Falcon 9 had roared off the pad at California's Vandenberg Space Force Base, hoisting a classified payload for the US Space Force. That mission underscores just how deeply the American military now leans on the private launch provider's capacity to get sensitive hardware into orbit.
A Government Finger on the Starshield Dial
The political dimension of SpaceX's business moved into sharper focus alongside the military launches. Reuters, citing Western government officials, reported that the order to restrict the Starshield service for Ukraine came directly from the White House. Kyiv had earlier said SpaceX throttled Starlink connectivity for terminals operating at high speeds, hampering several military operations. Elon Musk's response was blunt: Starshield answers to the US government, which also sets the limits on how it can be used. Decisions on speed caps and usage restrictions, he indicated, rest with the US military and the president.
For investors, that division of authority matters. The restrictions cannot be chalked up as a corporate decision alone, and a successful rocket flight does nothing to make the political headache disappear. It is a separate operational data point whose economic weight has to be judged apart from government-imposed usage rules.
Cargo Runs and a Push for More Launch Capacity
Away from the security missions, SpaceX kept its civilian freight schedule running. On October 13, the 35th Commercial Resupply Services mission for NASA launched with more than 6,300 pounds of cargo and scientific experiments bound for the International Space Station.
To expand the flight capacity needed over the long haul, regulatory reviews are underway for the company's own spaceport. Roughly a week ago, the FAA opened an environmental review for a plan to conduct up to 456 Starship launches per year at the Starbase site — far above the 25 flights currently permitted. The agency kicked off a public comment period and scheduled public hearings. Broader launch rights are a key lever for handling future heavy-lift transports for government customers and for the company's own satellite constellation at the scale it envisions.
Quarterly Scorecard Due After the Bell
Today, October 20, brings the financial reckoning. SpaceX has said it will release its financial and operational results for the third quarter of 2026 after the close of regular US trading, accompanied by an audio-only webcast at 15:30 CT, or 16:30 ET. The report offers the formal setting for a broader read on the business. The launches document missions carried out; the numbers are meant to shed light on how the company is actually performing. No firm conclusion about profitability follows from a rocket launch alone.
The stock closed yesterday at EUR 132.02, up 1.6 percent. With a market capitalization of EUR 1,968.56 billion, the valuation already reflects a dominant position in launch vehicles and tight integration with government programs.

articles.title: Is Russia stalking satellites which help Ukraine from space? - Al Jazeera
articles.summary: Is Russia stalking satellites which help Ukraine from space?  Al Jazeera
articles.full_text:
A Russian military satellite has manoeuvred to within metres of a US-registered radar satellite believed to provide intelligence to Ukraine, according to space-tracking data reported by The War Zone, a US defence news site.
Cosmos 2612 may have passed ICEYE-X36, a satellite owned by the US arm of the Finnish company ICEYE.
LeoLabs, a US space-tracking company, put the closest approach at about 500 metres, according to Breaking Defence.
ICEYE has supplied radar imagery to Ukraine since 2022, Defence News reported.
So is Russia stalking satellites which help Ukraine from space? Al Jazeera spoke to analysts to find out:
What has happened?
A Russian satellite has deliberately positioned itself close to a Western one, after months of manoeuvring.
Cosmos 2612 is one of six satellites the Russian military launched in April, The War Zone reported.
In May, four of them moved close to an ICEYE satellite.
ICEYE-X36 is a commercial satellite, owned by a private company rather than a government, but ICEYE sells radar imagery to militaries and supplies data to the US and its allies.
ICEYE’s chief executive, Rafal Modrzewski, told the Reuters news agency the company then moved its own satellite, which appeared to prompt further Russian manoeuvres.
Then, between Thursday and Friday last week, Cosmos 2612 closed in from more than 320km (200 miles) from ICEYE-X36 to about 4.8km (3 miles), the space-tracking company LeoLabs told the news site Axios.
Over the weekend, it moved between positions ahead of and behind the ICEYE satellite, at times coming within roughly 500 metres, LeoLabs said in a report on Monday, adding that the estimate was uncertain and, by Monday, it had begun to move away.
A Ukrainian official told Axios that Ukraine’s military works with ICEYE and uses its capabilities, but said it was unclear whether ICEYE-X36 itself supports Ukraine.
Has Russia done this before, and what is the purpose?
In the past, Russia has mainly carried out such manoeuvres against Western military satellites, rather than commercially owned ones, Mark Hilborne, a senior lecturer in the defence studies department at King’s College London, told Al Jazeera.
In early 2020, two Russian satellites moved close to USA 245, a US spy satellite.
In September 2025, German Defence Minister Boris Pistorius said two Russian Luch-Olymp satellites were tracking two Intelsat satellites used by the German military.
Dr Marco Langbroek, a lecturer in optical space situational awareness at TU Delft Faculty of Aerospace Engineering, said: “At geostationary altitude, we have seen two Russian satellites (LUCH/OLYMP-K 1 & 2) repeatedly approach western communication satellites to distances of a few tens of kilometres in the past few years, likely with the intention to eavesdrop on communications and data transfers. And we have seen the Russians practising very close approaches in Low Earth Orbit – similar to what they now did to ICEYE-X36 – with their own satellites as test targets.”
However, this incident is different, because “approaching another satellite this close without the cooperation of the owner or operator of the other satellite, is widely considered ‘not done’ as it is dangerous, with a risk of collision or interference.
“It is equivalent to placing your car on the freeway within 10 cm of another driving car: highly unsafe.”
Langbroek said it is not known what the purpose of the Russian manoeuvre was, however, “it could be a dry run for a future attack, it could be provocation or scare tactics to ruffle the feathers of Ukraine and its allies, and/or a test to see how the satellite operators react to a threat like this.”
This sort of manoeuvre, therefore, falls into the pattern of “hybrid warfare” – “the same kind of provocations and inciting reactions like what Russia does when they fly a drone into Polish airspace or zoom a NATO warship at low elevation in the Baltic Sea”.
How common are these incidents?
Close approaches have happened for years, but not like this.
Hilborne said this is “the first time that a country has done such a manoeuvre … against the commercial satellite without any consent”.
It was also “incredibly close”, he said, with some reports putting the distance at less than 30 metres.
Far more common is interference that does not require going near a satellite at all. This is mostly done through jamming, which drowns out a satellite’s signals, often from the ground.
Western military officials told Reuters that Russian interference with Western space systems has increased significantly since its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
What is the significance of this?
For Hilborne, the choice of target “is starting to indicate that Russia does not distinguish between commercial and military satellites as potential targets”.
That matters because militaries, including Ukraine’s, increasingly rely on commercial satellites for communications and imagery.
Moscow has warned about this.
In October 2022, a senior Russian foreign ministry official told the United Nations that “quasi-civilian infrastructure may be a legitimate target for a retaliatory strike”.
Juliana Suess, a space security researcher at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs (SWP) in Berlin, said Russia may be calculating that reactions will be less severe if it shadows a commercial satellite rather than a sovereign one, especially one not belonging to the US.
But ownership is not that simple.
ICEYE-X36 is owned by ICEYE’s US subsidiary and registered as a US satellite, Hilborne noted, adding, “this creates a complex problem”.
The distance matters too. A gap of less than 5km may sound far, Suess said, but “it’s essentially a hop and a skip in space”.
“It’s incredibly close and could potentially enable Russia to conduct nefarious activity, including intercepting data from the satellite or disrupting its service – temporarily via signal jamming, for example,” she added.
“A kinetic attack would also be possible but seems less likely at this point in time, in part because this would be an unprecedented measure taken against a satellite”, she explained.
Is Russia just sending a message, or escalating?
Probably both.
“It is sending a message that these platforms could be held under threat,” Hilborne said, adding that it also represents an escalation, suggesting Russia might be willing to attack, since any satellite could be used as a weapon simply by crashing it into another.
Suess added: “I think regardless of whether we see further manoeuvring or consequences, the political goal of intimidation should not be underestimated”.
“The manoeuvre is also a message that space assets cannot be considered wholly safe or removed from the war in Ukraine”, she said.
She pointed to November 2021, when Russia destroyed one of its own satellites with a missile, an event referred to in the European Union’s 2023 space strategy.
“We have long known what Russia is capable of in terms of disrupting or even destroying space assets. This manoeuvre is also a reminder of those previously demonstrated capabilities,” she said.
Moscow calls such spacecraft “inspector satellites”, and in 2020 described such manoeuvres as common practice “by many countries”, Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty reported.
Hilborne described the approach as “another example of activity that sits below the threshold of conflict”.
An outright attack on ICEYE-X36 looks unlikely for now, Hilborne said.
“With the current balance in the conflict, and this being an American-registered satellite, it would seem unlikely that Russia would actually attack the satellite, as the response would be unpredictable”, he said.
An attack could also create a large amount of space debris, which would be a problem for everyone, he added, warning that “it’s hard to second-guess where Russia draws the line”.
How has Ukraine fought to keep its eyes in space?
Ukraine’s access to satellites has come under pressure before, at times from its own allies.
In March 2025, as Washington paused intelligence sharing with Kyiv, the US National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency “temporarily suspended” Ukraine’s access to the main portal for US government-purchased commercial imagery.
If ICEYE-X36 were disrupted, Ukraine would not necessarily go blind, Suess said, because the ICEYE constellation has more than one satellite, and sovereign radar satellites, such as Germany’s, could also provide data.
But speed is the issue. According to ICEYE, the expanded access agreed this year meant faster access, Suess explained.
“The question is whether a similarly fast transfer of data could be enabled with a new provider, whether commercial or sovereign in nature,” she said.
Now, Ukraine faces another squeeze. Last week, the order to limit Starshield – the military-grade version of SpaceX’s Starlink service – for Ukraine came from inside the White House, two US officials and a Western official told Reuters.
On Saturday, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Starshield is currently unavailable to Ukraine, but that Kyiv’s request to use it for attacks deep inside Russia is “under discussion”.

articles.title: ByteDance, Alibaba, Tencent Order Over 3 Million Nvidia Chips Worth $35 Billion - Arise News
articles.summary: ByteDance, Alibaba, Tencent Order Over 3 Million Nvidia Chips Worth $35 Billion  Arise News
articles.full_text:
ByteDance, Alibaba and Tencent have ordered more than three million of Nvidia’s new RTX PRO 5500 graphics cards, valued at over $35 billion, as Chinese technology companies seek powerful computing chips that comply with US export restrictions.
Two people familiar with the matter told Reuters that the orders, which have not been previously reported, reflect growing demand for Nvidia hardware in China despite Washington’s restrictions on advanced semiconductor exports.
The US-based chipmaker has reportedly warned customers and partners that it cannot guarantee full deliveries because demand from Chinese technology companies far exceeds planned production.
One source said Nvidia indicated that customers might receive only five to 10 per cent of the quantities requested. Another said the company expected to produce no more than three million RTX PRO 5500 cards globally in 2027, while total orders from Chinese customers have exceeded six million.
The three technology giants’ orders are priced at approximately $11,400 per card, giving them a potential combined value of more than $35 billion, according to two of the sources, who requested anonymity because they were not authorised to speak to the media.
The RTX PRO 5500 is a workstation graphics chip designed for high-performance professional computers rather than the large data-centre clusters used to run Nvidia’s most advanced artificial intelligence processors. However, it is among the most powerful Nvidia chips currently available to Chinese buyers.
Nvidia’s Blackwell-based B300 data-centre chip is barred from sale to Chinese customers under US export controls, while exports of its Hopper-based H200 processor are subject to case-by-case reviews and licensing conditions.
Chinese technology companies are seeking to use the RTX PRO 5500 primarily for AI inference, the process through which trained models generate responses to user prompts. Inference generally requires less computing power than training AI models on massive datasets.
The surge in demand highlights the pressure on computing capacity in China, where companies are racing to develop advanced AI models and expand the technology’s use across industries.
Nvidia Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang has said US restrictions reduced the company’s share of China’s AI data-centre chip market from near-monopoly levels to effectively zero. However, demand for the RTX PRO 5500 suggests that less powerful products that remain accessible could provide Nvidia with another route into the Chinese market.
Washington’s export controls have encouraged Chinese companies to seek alternatives from domestic suppliers, while Beijing has promoted the use of locally manufactured chips. Huawei has gained market share, although Chinese chipmakers have generally struggled to match leading American products, partly because restrictions have limited their access to advanced semiconductor manufacturing equipment.
An Nvidia spokesperson said Chinese producers of workstation chips and graphics cards had experienced “unprecedented growth since 2022,” when the restrictions were first imposed.
The spokesperson added that US companies remained constrained by a combination of what Nvidia described as outdated American export controls and China’s own restrictions on US imports.
ByteDance, Alibaba and Tencent did not respond to requests for comment. The US Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security and China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology also did not respond.
Nvidia’s reported inability to guarantee deliveries reflects both rising demand and its manufacturing priorities.
Two sources said Nvidia was expected to allocate much of its production capacity at Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company to Rubin, its next-generation platform for large-scale data centres, from 2027, rather than products such as the RTX PRO 5500.
Nvidia has reportedly told customers to expect early samples in December, with commercial deliveries scheduled to begin in the first quarter of 2027. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company declined to comment.
The RTX PRO 5500 is similar in performance to Nvidia’s RTX 6000D, a reduced-capability product launched last year to comply with US export restrictions.
Chinese technology companies initially showed limited interest in the RTX 6000D, with some declining to place orders because they considered the chips too expensive for their capabilities and expected Washington to permit sales of more powerful processors.
However, those expectations have diminished as restrictions have persisted and AI computing capacity has remained scarce, making the RTX PRO 5500 a more attractive alternative, two sources said.
One source said the RTX 6000D had since been discontinued and its market price in China had doubled.
Separately, Shenzhen-listed fintech and AI-computing services company Tansun Technology disclosed in an October 13 filing that it had agreed to purchase 20,000 RTX PRO 5500 cards from an unidentified counterparty.
The company warned that supply shortages, strong industry demand and overseas technology restrictions could delay deliveries or reduce the quantity supplied.

articles.title: Intel asks FCC for waiver to buy foreign robots — chipmaker’s automated guided vehicles could run afoul of agency’s sweeping robot ban - Tom's Hardware
articles.summary: Intel asks FCC for waiver to buy foreign robots — chipmaker’s automated guided vehicles could run afoul of agency’s sweeping robot ban  Tom's Hardware
articles.full_text:
Intel has asked the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) to make an exception for the automated guided vehicles (AGVs) that the company uses to transport the sensitive silicon wafers and other materials, containers, and supplies needed to make the most advanced chips in its fabs. According to Bloomberg, the American chipmaker fears that its AGVs would fall under the blanket prohibition against foreign-made robots after they were added to the FCC’s Covered List.
AGVs are niche machines that chip fabs use to transport materials and supplies between tools and sections of the fab, helping ensure that the cleanroom conditions required for each manufacturing process are maintained. This makes them critical equipment for U.S. semiconductor manufacturing, but, apparently, there are no suitable domestic alternatives for these devices at the moment. Intel’s current fleet of AGVs requires continuous maintenance, including software and firmware updates, and if it’s forced to find a local supplier for its AGVs, the company says that it would take years, crippling the United States’ chipmaking efforts.
The biggest AGV suppliers are Japanese companies like Murata Machinery and Daifuku Co., while a few smaller businesses from South Korea and Taiwan are also trying to break into the market. It’s unclear why these companies haven’t applied for a conditional approval yet, which would allow them to continue selling these products in the U.S. while also promising Washington that they’ll set up a manufacturing base in the country. This is something that Netgear has already done, allowing it to continue selling its foreign-made routers despite being an American company.
Intel says that it remains unclear if updates to its AGVs would break compliance with the FCC, and that it’s asking the agency to issue a conditional waiver “out of an abundance of caution to ensure the ongoing operation of these specific AGV units.” While Team Blue is the only company concerned about AGVs at the moment, other chip manufacturers would likely need a similar waiver in the near future, especially as they build more fabs in the U.S. This includes TSMC, which is planning to build 12 more fabs and four packaging facilities in Arizona, Samsung, with its new Taylor, Texas, fab, and even Elon Musk’s Terafab, which has already begun construction.
Washington has been using the FCC to force companies to invest in American manufacturing. Its blanket bans on foreign-made products like drones and routers have affected some of the biggest brands in the U.S., including DJI and TP-Link. While these bans do not outright ban the sale of all products made by these companies, especially those that have already been approved before, they make it impossible for them to introduce new products and even release software updates to their existing product line. The FCC eventually walked back on the software update ban, but they still would not be able to register new products unless they build them in the U.S.

articles.title: [New Space Odyssey] Walker in Space CEO Kim Hae-dong targets 2029 launch of VEROS-1 robotic satellite to repair billion‑dollar GEO assets - DongA Science
