[Editor’s note] With the establishment of the Korea Aerospace Administration and the successful launch of the Korean launch vehicle ‘Nuri’, Korean space companies are pressing ahead on the front line of ‘New Space’, where private companies lead space development. We take a close, on-site look at the efforts of Korean space companies that are leveraging their unique strengths to expand their presence not only in Korea but also in the global space market.
“We are entering an era when satellites that used to be untouchable once they went up can now be repaired and reused in space. Since last year, the entire paradigm of satellite manufacturing and operation has been changing.”
At Walker in Space’s headquarters in Sejong, CEO Kim Hae-dong described the recent changes sweeping through the space industry and clearly laid out Walker in Space’s vision. Walker in Space is an on‑orbit servicing (OOS, On‑Orbit Servicing) company founded in 2024.
OOS is a service in which a spacecraft approaches a satellite in space that has broken down or run out of fuel, captures it, then refuels or repairs it. It is essentially the space equivalent of a car repair shop on Earth or aerial refueling for aircraft.
Kim is one of Korea’s leading experts in the space sector, having spent more than 30 years researching space technology at the Korea Aerospace Research Institute (KARI) and Hyundai Space and Aircraft. He took part in developing the control system for Korea’s first practical satellite, Arirang‑1.
At KARI, he studied space debris collision analysis and capture technologies, making him one of Korea’s “first‑generation space debris researchers.” In 2007, when China destroyed one of its retired satellites with a missile, generating massive space debris, he began full‑scale research on space debris while assessing collision risks to Korean satellites.
Kim’s research led to technologies for removing space debris and then expanded into “technologies that save satellites before they become debris.” He explained, “The market where people say they’ll pay you to clean up debris is still a long way off, but there are already people willing to pay if you can save a satellite worth hundreds of billions of won.”
● Walker in Space’s main customers: ‘heavyweight’ satellites in geostationary orbit
Walker in Space’s primary targets are geostationary satellites. Geostationary orbit lies about 36,000 km above Earth’s equator; satellites there orbit at the same rate as Earth’s rotation and therefore appear fixed over a single point on the ground.
Recently, the space industry has been shifting toward launching large constellations of relatively inexpensive satellites, as exemplified by SpaceX’s ‘Starlink’. Starlink satellites operate in low Earth orbit at altitudes of a few hundred kilometers, with each satellite costing tens of billions of won. If one fails, it is more economical to launch a new satellite than to repair it in space.
Geostationary satellites, however, are high‑value assets that can cost hundreds of billions of won each. Even if the satellite itself has no technical issues, once its fuel is depleted and it can no longer maintain its assigned orbital slot, it becomes difficult to operate. Launching a replacement satellite entails enormous expense. That is why technology to extend the life of existing satellites is needed.
Kim drew an analogy to the automobile market. “Geostationary orbit is like a highway for big, expensive luxury cars, whereas low orbit is full of compact cars,” he said. “Just as the advent of compact cars doesn’t make luxury cars disappear, there is a distinct market for large, high‑value satellites.”
Satellite design philosophy has changed as well. In the past, engineers assumed satellites could not be repaired in space, so they installed spare parts and designed them to minimize failure risks. That naturally drove up manufacturing costs.
Now that repairs in space are becoming possible, satellites can be built without carrying spare parts, thereby lowering unit costs. “If we used to spend 500 billion won on a single satellite to last 10 years,” Kim said, “it is now more economical to build one for 200–300 billion won, operate it for five years, and then extend the remaining five years through services in space.”
● OOS once dismissed as a “20–30 year out market” gains momentum in just a year
Kim recalls that around 2015, when he began working in the OOS field, most people saw it as “a market to think about maybe 20–30 years down the road.” The mood shifted starting late last year.
“Even just last year, domestic satellite operators would say, ‘Develop the technology first and we’ll contact you later,’” Kim said. “But starting this year, they began approaching us first to ask when the service could be available.” When they explored overseas providers for satellite servicing, they found that conditions were restrictive and required handing over all of their satellite data.
“Perceptions in the defense sector are changing as well,” he added. OOS is a quintessential dual‑use technology for both civilian and military purposes. If a spacecraft can approach a satellite and extend its life, it can also use a robotic arm to damage components and disable it, or draw close for surveillance.
“The U.S. Department of Defense is directly investing in startups and companies in this field,” Kim said. “There have already been real cases where Russian and Chinese satellites approached U.S. satellites, took images, and then fled.”
In Korea, awareness of the need to secure OOS technologies for defense applications is also growing. “The Ministry of National Defense had initially targeted around 2040 for securing satellite life‑extension and repair technologies,” Kim explained, “but recently it has begun to recognize the need to acquire such capabilities earlier.”
This year, the ministry launched a planning and research project on a ‘defense satellite life‑extension system’. Walker in Space was selected for the project in August and will carry out research through December. “It’s inefficient for the military to launch a dedicated servicing satellite just to fix one satellite,” Kim said. “A structure in which private companies validate the technologies and the military then purchases the services will be far more cost‑effective.”
● The No. 2 spot in OOS is still open… “We’ll compete with humanoid arms and artificial intelligence (AI)”
Currently, the only company that effectively provides OOS as a commercial service is the U.S. firm Northrop Grumman. Its servicing satellite ‘MEV‑1’, launched in 2019, successfully docked with a communications satellite the following year to help maintain its orbit. This approach—attaching to a satellite and taking over station‑keeping—is less technically demanding than directly refueling, yet even that has not been implemented by other companies so far, Kim noted.
“The second‑place spot is still vacant,” he said. “Around five or six companies, including Japan’s Astroscale and U.S. firms Starfish Space and Infinite Orbits, are preparing demonstration satellite launches this year and next, all vying for that No. 2 position.” He predicted, “After 2030, receiving services in orbit will become commonplace, and the market will really open up.”
Walker in Space differentiates itself from competitors in two key areas: precision and cost‑effectiveness. While other companies typically use clamping arms that simply grab the target, Walker in Space’s goal is to integrate humanoid‑type robotic arms capable of performing a wide range of delicate tasks, along with AI.
They plan to use AI in conjunction with lidar and vision sensors to rapidly identify the shape of the target satellite and train the system to capture misaligned satellites without causing damage. Ultimately, the aim is to enable the satellite’s onboard computer to autonomously make decisions throughout the approach and capture sequence.
Robotic arms for space use are extremely expensive abroad. Walker in Space intends to adapt industrial robotic arms designed for terrestrial use by reinforcing them so they can withstand the space environment for two to three years. This approach mirrors Starlink’s strategy of using off‑the‑shelf terrestrial components to reduce satellite costs. “If we can lower production costs,” Kim said, “we could even carry spare robotic arms and replace them in orbit when they fail.”
He expressed confidence about the threat of latecomers. “Investors often ask whether companies that have been making satellites for a long time or those that have built many robots could quickly catch up if they enter this field,” he said. “My answer is, ‘Let them try.’”
Even if a company has experience in both satellite manufacturing and robot development, simply combining the two does not guarantee the ability to perform precise operations in space. “You need software and hardware specifically designed for operating robotic arms in the space environment,” Kim explained. “If you start without any prior research in that area, it will take at least five years.”
● Series A funding by year’s end, VEROS‑1 launch in 2029… “Aiming for global top three in OOS”
Walker in Space has completed the first phase of overall system design for its servicing robotic satellite and is now moving into the phase of selecting component suppliers.

It will house a large clean room, thermal and vibration test equipment for simulating the space environment, a space robotics test lab, and a satellite control room. The robotic arm capture simulations currently conducted via digital twins at headquarters will be expanded there.

articles.full_text:
Alphabet GOOGL said Google demonstrated a method for reducing errors in a key quantum-computing process on its Willow processor, advancing work toward more reliable machines.
The technique, called magic-state cultivation, produced specially prepared quantum states with 99.99% logical fidelity, a measure of how reliably they preserve the intended quantum information. Google researchers said the method reduced errors about 40-fold compared with states produced without cultivation.
These states enable operations needed for complex quantum calculations, but generating them can consume substantial computing resources. The process checks candidate states for errors and discards unsuccessful attempts, retaining only those that pass the checks.
The team also transferred cultivated states between two error-correction methods, known as color codes and surface codes. That result suggests the approach can work across different ways of protecting quantum information. The research was published Oct. 15 in Science.
The findings do not establish that Google has built a commercially practical quantum computer. Researchers said the technique must be demonstrated at a larger scale, and engineering challenges remain before it can support useful, fault-tolerant machines.

articles.title: Google Willow Breakthrough: Could Quantum Computing Unlock Satoshi-Era Bitcoin Wallets? - Analytics Insight
articles.summary: Google Willow Breakthrough: Could Quantum Computing Unlock Satoshi-Era Bitcoin Wallets?  Analytics Insight
articles.full_text:
Google's latest quantum computing breakthrough has renewed concerns about Bitcoin security, particularly dormant wallets associated with Satoshi Nakamoto. Although current quantum computers can't break Bitcoin's cryptography, recent research shows why developers are preparing stronger protections.
On October 15, Google announced progress in magic state cultivation, a technique supporting advanced quantum calculations. According to Google, its Willow processor reduced errors by about 40-fold and achieved 99.99% accuracy on successfully prepared states.
However, only 8% of preparation attempts succeeded, demonstrating substantial technical limitations. The improvement concerns quantum error correction, not Bitcoin private-key recovery. Willow contains 105 physical qubits, far below the capabilities expected for practical attacks against cryptocurrency signatures.
Bitcoin uses elliptic-curve cryptography to authorize transactions. A sufficiently powerful quantum computer running Shor's algorithm could theoretically derive private keys from exposed public keys. Early pay-to-public-key outputs reveal public keys directly, making some dormant holdings particularly relevant. Address reuse creates additional exposure, while certain newer wallet formats also reveal public keys.
According to Glassnode's assessment, approximately 1.92 million BTC occupy structurally exposed addresses, while another 4.12 million BTC face exposure through wallet practices. Together, these categories represent approximately 6.04 million BTC, although estimates differ across research methodologies. An estimated 1.1 million BTC is associated with Satoshi Nakamoto, but ownership remains unconfirmed.
On October 15, the Quantum Alliance announced cooperation among nine blockchain organizations, including Quantus, Keystone, Abelian, Hacken and Postquant Labs.
The initiative focuses on quantum-resistant wallets, blockchain upgrades and common security standards.
Its Quantum Doom Clock identifies March 2028 as an early potential threat window. However, this represents a projection rather than evidence that cryptographically capable quantum computers will exist by then. Researchers continue debating how quickly fault-tolerant quantum hardware could develop.
On October 13, Coinbase emphasized the importance of preparing Bitcoin for post-quantum cryptography. The exchange identified BIP-360 and P2TRv2 among potential technical approaches, while supporting gradual migration toward stronger wallet protection.
Coinbase also highlighted complications involving dormant holdings, describing coins that ‘cannot or will not move’ as ‘a separate governance and engineering problem.’ These holdings present challenges because their owners may lack the private keys required to transfer funds.
For existing Bitcoin holders, avoiding unnecessary address reuse can reduce certain forms of public-key exposure. Nevertheless, moving funds does not automatically provide quantum resistance, because current Bitcoin signatures remain vulnerable in principle.
Any transition would require technical testing, community agreement and reliable migration procedures. Developers must also consider transaction costs, wallet compatibility and the treatment of permanently inaccessible coins.
Google's Willow breakthrough advances quantum computing but does not enable attackers to unlock Satoshi-era wallets today. The challenge is preparing Bitcoin's cryptographic infrastructure before quantum computers become sufficiently powerful. Coordinated upgrades and early planning remain essential for protecting digital assets.
Also Read: EU Regulators Put Quantum Risk on Crypto Custody & Bank Agenda
1. Can Google's Willow quantum chip unlock Satoshi-era Bitcoin wallets?
Google's Willow chip cannot currently recover Bitcoin private keys or access Satoshi-era wallets because it lacks the capabilities required to break Bitcoin's cryptography. However, sufficiently powerful future quantum computers could theoretically threaten wallets with exposed public keys.
2. How does quantum computing threaten Bitcoin wallet security?
A sufficiently advanced quantum computer could use Shor's algorithm to derive private keys from publicly exposed elliptic-curve public keys. This could potentially allow attackers to authorize unauthorized transactions from vulnerable Bitcoin wallets.
3. How much Bitcoin could be vulnerable to future quantum attacks?
According to Glassnode's assessment cited in the article, approximately 1.92 million BTC are held in structurally exposed addresses, while another 4.12 million BTC face exposure through wallet practices. Together, these categories represent roughly 6.04 million BTC potentially exposed to future quantum threats, not funds currently accessible to attackers.
4. What is the Quantum Alliance, and how is it protecting cryptocurrencies?
The Quantum Alliance is a collaboration of nine blockchain organizations working on quantum-resistant wallets, security standards, and blockchain infrastructure upgrades. Its initiatives aim to help cryptocurrency networks prepare for potential threats from advanced quantum computing technologies.
5. What steps are Coinbase and Bitcoin developers taking against quantum threats?
Coinbase has supported phased adoption of post-quantum cryptography and highlighted proposals such as BIP-360 and P2TRv2 as possible security approaches. Developers are also examining migration strategies for existing wallets, although dormant Bitcoin holdings and inaccessible private keys present significant challenges.

articles.full_text:
OpenBSD 8.0 is here, marking the project's 61st release and continuing its schedule of semiannual releases dating back to 1996. What started more than 30 years ago as a fork of NetBSD has grown into one of the most security-conscious operating systems in active development. In a post to the project's announcements mailing list, OpenBSD founder Theo de Raadt highlights a host of improvements included with the latest version and writes that the project remains "proud of OpenBSD's record of more than thirty years with only two remote holes in the default install."
The latest OpenBSD version brings new features and improvements across the board. These changes, particularly the new Intel Arc support and expanded virtual address space, should improve compatibility with modern graphics cards and allow the system to map more than 4GB of VRAM. Some of the major updates noted in the release newsletter are as follows:

Added support for Intel Arc A-Series (DG2/Alchemist) graphics cards.
512GB kernel virtual address space on AMD64, up from 4GB, allowing VRAM mapping above 4GB.
Added hibernation support for ARM64 systems.
A new RPKI-to-router daemon: rtrd(8).
RISC-V improvements including kernel support for the 'V' vector extension and support for Advanced Interrupt Architecture.
Wireless network driver additions and improvements, including 802.11n and 40 MHz channels for the qwx(4) wireless driver.
Added support for up to 64 virtual CPUs per guest virtual machine.
Security and internal improvements for LibreSSL 4.4.0 and OpenSSH 10.6.
Improvements to the vmm/vmd virtualization stack.

The new OpenBSD also retires support for Loongson architecture after the port stopped working with the Clang 22 compiler. If you're interested in reading over all the changes that come with the new OpenBSD 8.0, you can take a look at the release announcement.Read full article

Vast new fossil record challenges story of Earth’s ‘big five’ mass extinctions
An artificial-intelligence model trained on nearly four million fossils suggests that three of the extinction events might have happened more gradually than previously thought.
Large language models (LLMs) such as OpenAI’s ChatGPT are trained to recognize patterns in written texts, helping them to choose a statistically probable word to complete a sentence. Palaeontologists have now trained a similar model on fossil records instead of words, then used it to reconstruct a timeline of changes in Earth’s biodiversity over hundreds of millions of years in unprecedented detail.
This big-data approach to interpreting the rock record — the field known as stratigraphy — could spur a rethink of major upheavals in the history of life, the model’s developers say. For instance, the model suggests that three of the “Big Five” mass-extinction events were gradual declines in biodiversity, rather than the sudden cataclysms described by other reconstructions.
The model is “a real revolution for studying stratigraphy and past diversity change”, says Shuzhong Shen, a palaeontologist at Nanjing University in China, who presented the research at a meeting of the Geological Society of America in Denver, Colorado, on 12 October.
Other researchers say that although the model’s reconstruction — called OneStrata — seems to be the most detailed global record so far, scientists already have high-resolution reconstructions of changes in biodiversity at specific locations, including many that shed light on mass extinctions.
“We could do some extra things with it, but I don’t know if it would be Earth shattering,” says Matthew Clapham, a palaeontologist at the University of California, Santa Cruz.
Strata struggles
The history of life is written in the fossil record. Researchers can reconstruct the grand story of adaptation and extinction across Earth’s history by marking the depth at which species occur in layers of sedimentary rock, called strata; depth corresponds to when a fossil was deposited in geological time. However, it is a steep computational problem to combine sequences from many different sites involving tens of thousands of species into a single coherent timeline of changing biodiversity.
To simplify this task, stratigraphers divide sequences of fossils for each species into time intervals of millions of years. This makes it easier to assemble many sequences into a unified whole. But it produces a blurry view, obscuring changes in biodiversity that occur over shorter time intervals.
For the past two decades, Shen and his colleagues have worked to get a sharper picture by compiling a huge data set of fossils and other geological data called OneStratigraphy. This includes data on the depth of millions of fossil specimens in sequences of rock from tens of thousands of sites around the world.
Large fossil model
In 2020, Shen and his colleagues ran an algorithmic method on a supercomputer to piece together thousands of these sequences, enabling them to estimate when a species appeared and went extinct with a resolution of 26,000 years — much higher than the resolution of previous estimates. They could then reconstruct a high-resolution timeline for 11,000 marine species over about 300 million years1. However, including more species at shorter intervals requires an impractical amount of computational resources.
To get around that computational limit, Shen’s colleagues at the Zhejiang Lab — an AI-focused research institution in Hangzhou, China — used data from OneStratigraphy to train a machine-learning model on statistical patterns in the fossil record. Just as an LLM uses its training to predict the next word in a sentence, the OneStrata model uses those patterns to predict when a particular fossil is most likely to have been deposited.

In corporate America, Stanley Anderson ’79 says, executives often assume that their peers grew up in privileged circumstances. 



He did not.



“I spent my early years trying not to get recruited into gangs, getting shot at, watching my friends get murdered, and thinking that if I don’t leave, I will die,” says Anderson, who was raised in Chicago. “I was fortunate to survive.”



But he thrived, building an impressive career at the likes of HP, Intel, and the Palo Alto Research Center. Now he is applying his management expertise as CEO of Costa Pickleball, a Las Vegas–based startup that sells high-performance paddles in decorative designs. Beyond giving customers a way to, as he says, “bring their identity to the court,” he is also betting on technology: He’s developing a quieter type of paddle he expects will provide a competitive advantage. 



Succeeding in today’s pickleball market will be tough, but Anderson thinks he has what it takes, partly thanks to an important lesson he learned at MIT: “There’s nothing you can’t accomplish if you are willing to put effort into it.”

articles.full_text:
It has been 13 years since the debut of a new medium-lift rocket in the United States, the Antares vehicle developed by Orbital Sciences Corporation.
The initial 100-series variant of the Antares rocket was kind of a hot mess. The rocket used old Soviet engines built during the era when Apollo astronauts were landing on the Moon. Decades later, in the 1990s, Aerojet acquired the engines and refurbished them for a rocket that would launch in the 2010s. Predictably, on the fifth launch of an Antares rocket in 2014, it exploded.
The Antares vehicle is the last of a dying breed of medium-lift rockets—defined as having a lift capacity of 2 to 20 metric tons—in the United States. Nearly a decade and a half later there is a new generation of medium-lift vehicles coming online, and they are starkly different from Antares, which had not just Russian engines but a core stage manufactured in Ukraine.Read full article

articles.title: It’s a bird, it’s a plane … it’s a robo-puffin?
articles.summary: Given that water is 1,000 times denser than air, moving through those two mediums requires very different mechanics—or so one might assume. Yet birds like gulls and puffins can plunge into the sea, swim underwater, and leap back into the air to fly away. And now engineers at MIT and EPFL in Lausanne, Switzerland, have…
articles.full_text:
Given that water is 1,000 times denser than air, moving through those two mediums requires very different mechanics—or so one might assume. Yet birds like gulls and puffins can plunge into the sea, swim underwater, and leap back into the air to fly away. And now engineers at MIT and EPFL in Lausanne, Switzerland, have designed a robot that can do likewise. 



The “flapping-wing aerial-aquatic vehicle,” or FAAV, weighs less than 300 grams (about half a pound) and is equipped with a central fuselage, two flexible wings, and a steerable tail. The body contains a battery and a waterproof electric motor that drives a crankshaft, which pumps the wings up and down at preset frequencies. The wings are made of thin membranes that are coated with hydrophobic nanoparticles to help wick away water. And the tail is motorized, enabling it to change its angle to help the robot fly up or dive down.



In experiments carried out in a water tank and at Lake Geneva, a team led by Raphael Zufferey, an assistant professor of mechanical engineering at MIT, identified combinations of wing size, flapping frequency, and tail angle that enable the robot to smoothly transition from swimming to flying. 



The best results came with medium-size wings that were flexible enough to minimize flapping amplitude in water and also firm enough to keep the robot aloft in the air. The speeds and flapping frequencies were similar to those used by actual birds, and a pitch of 70 degrees—a relatively steep angle—allowed the robot to make the leap from water to air. Interestingly, although many diving birds paddle their feet to help them take off from the water’s surface, the team found that the bot didn’t need feet at all.



The engineers’ results could help pave the way for a new class of drones and vehicles that could fly to and sample from aquatic regions too dangerous for traditional vessels to access.



“Our dream vision is for oceanographers, marine biologists, and members of coastal communities to launch this robot from a boat, or from shore, and it would fly close to the area of interest, such as an iceberg or a port facility, or over a pod of whales,” says Zufferey. “It would dive into the water to take a measurement or collect a sample, and fly back to deliver the data at a fraction of the cost of traditional methods. Then it could go back out to dive for more.” 









The researchers are now trying to design wings that can turn as well as flap. They will also test the robot’s performance under turbulent conditions, such as swimming in choppy waters and flying through wind. Then they hope to deploy the vehicle to help answer questions in ocean science.



“One of the major challenges in ocean science is collecting data both frequently and across many locations, which is something this robot could do in the future,” Zufferey says. “You could send this out not just every week, but every hour. It could fly out at high speeds, dive in, fly back, deliver its data, and go back out, multiple times.”

articles.title: Here’s the tea
articles.summary: When Tristan Brown, an associate professor of history at MIT, first examined a Chinese tea chest label displayed at Old South Meeting House, he had no reason to doubt its story. Descendants of the Boston blacksmith Thomas Wells had donated the label in 1987, saying it had been recovered after colonial protesters threw tea into…
articles.full_text:
When Tristan Brown, an associate professor of history at MIT, first examined a Chinese tea chest label displayed at Old South Meeting House, he had no reason to doubt its story. Descendants of the Boston blacksmith Thomas Wells had donated the label in 1987, saying it had been recovered after colonial protesters threw tea into Boston Harbor in 1773. 



But after a year of research, Brown reached a different conclusion: The label was made nearly a century later. The decisive clue came when he read the Chinese text in Cantonese rather than Mandarin, as previous scholars had done. He found that the characters had been used phonetically, in slightly variant forms across contemporary sources, to represent the name of Smith, Archer & Co., a US firm that acquired Asian tea for shipment to American markets during the 1860s and 1870s.



COURTESY OF MIT GLOBAL HUMANITIES




Working with the Wells family, he traced the label to a relative who traveled from Michigan to California during the Gold Rush era before returning and operating a business known as the California Tea Store. Brown argues that claims for its revolutionary pedigree probably developed later, amid the centennial commemorations of the 1870s.



The discovery does not make the label historically insignificant, he says. Instead, what began as an inquiry into a supposed artifact of the Boston Tea Party became a study of how ordinary objects acquire historical authority, and how historical memory itself is made.



“History is never finished,” he says. “Even objects that have sat in museums for decades can reveal entirely new stories when we ask new questions.”

articles.title: Melt it, spin it, use it again
articles.summary: The average American throws out around 81 pounds of clothing each year, and there are few options for recycling it. MIT engineers hope to cut down on that textile waste with a new type of yarn.  The thermoplastic yarn mimics the properties of conventional elastic yarns, which typically combine spandex with polyester or nylon. Those…
articles.full_text:
The average American throws out around 81 pounds of clothing each year, and there are few options for recycling it. MIT engineers hope to cut down on that textile waste with a new type of yarn. 



The thermoplastic yarn mimics the properties of conventional elastic yarns, which typically combine spandex with polyester or nylon. Those fibers would have to be separated for recycling—a process that isn’t practical. But the MIT team found a way to create a similarly stretchy yarn from two variations of polyethylene, a material commonly used in milk jugs and grocery bags. Because they come from the same chemical family, the yarn can be melted as is. Svetlana Boriskina, who led the work as a research scientist in the Department of Mechanical Engineering, says a garment made from this material could then be spun into new yarn for a next generation of clothing. Even after 10 cycles of melting and respinning, the yarn stays as strong and flexible as conventional thread. 



“Now we have something that can be knitted and woven,” Boriskina says. “That is the next stage.” Someday, the researchers hope, a polyethylene garment could be dropped in a collection bin and sent to a recycling facility, promoting a more sustainable, circular textile economy.

articles.title: A reason to eat carbs
articles.summary: A high-fat, low-carbohydrate diet can help some people lose weight, and some research has shown that it may protect against colon cancer. But a new study suggests that such a ketogenic diet may also increase the risk of cancer in the small intestine. This type of diet forces the body to burn fatty acids instead…
articles.full_text:
A high-fat, low-carbohydrate diet can help some people lose weight, and some research has shown that it may protect against colon cancer. But a new study suggests that such a ketogenic diet may also increase the risk of cancer in the small intestine.



This type of diet forces the body to burn fatty acids instead of carbohydrates for fuel, producing by-products called ketone bodies. One of these, BHB, was thought to be responsible for the protective effect observed against colon cancer.



Omer Yilmaz, director of the MIT Stem Cell Initiative, worked with colleagues including MIT postdocs Jessica Shay and Fangtao Chi to investigate whether the effects were similar in the small intestine. But instead, they found that mice on a ketogenic diet were more likely to develop tumors in that part of the gastrointestinal system than those on a control diet were. 



Additional studies revealed that this tumor growth was driven by the way intestinal cells burn dietary fat for energy—a metabolic pathway called fatty acid oxidation. This pathway activates proteins that signal stem cells to multiply more rapidly. 



“Having more stem cells means that when you injure the small intestine, it can repair itself better, but the downside is that having more active stem cells can lead to tumor formation,” Yilmaz says.



Though the researchers confirmed that a ketogenic diet suppressed the development of colon tumors, their findings suggest that ketone bodies are not involved. “These molecules are essentially metabolic bystanders,” Yilmaz says.



One implication is that commercial ketone supplements probably do little to either help or harm people who take them. But the deeper issue is “why the same diet has opposite consequences in two adjacent parts of the gut,” Chi says. “That is what we are working to understand next.”



Whatever they discover, as Yilmaz says, “the message here is that we need to be very careful in generalizing the effects that these diets can have.”

These are images of quizzes I took in 3.091, Introduction to Solid-State Chemistry, in the fall of 1980.



One is my very first exam at MIT, and getting 49 out of 100 was a soul-crushing experience. I can still picture the TA, Leszek Pawlowicz, PhD ’87, returning my paper. He had a big smile on his face, and he said something to the effect of “I expect to see you double your score on the next quiz!” 



Well, I got the message. Studying at MIT was not like studying in high school, but I got 100 on the next quiz and graduated with good enough grades to get me into grad school. All it took, it seems, was that initial kick in the seat of my pants, then a kind hand helping me up off the ground.



Recently, I connected with Leszek, and he replied with a charming note. It felt good to let him know how much his encouragement meant to me. A good TA can really have lasting impact!

Growing up on a small farm in Nebraska, Megan Donahue ’85 discovered the wider world by reading her way through her local library. Today, she is learning how the wider universe works by studying galaxy clusters.



Donahue discovered her passion for physics in that library at age 12 and started her path into astronomy thanks to “a providential interaction.” Through MIT’s Undergraduate Research Opportunities Program, she got introduced to cutting-edge x-ray imaging—work she found “really cool.”



Now a professor of physics and astronomy at Michigan State University, she researches galaxy clusters and baryonic matter (matter made of protons and neutrons, as opposed to dark matter) in an effort to learn more about the composition of the universe and its evolution.



“Clusters of galaxies are very large scoops of the universe,” says Donahue, who served as president of the American Astronomical Society from 2018 to 2020. “It’s like taking a sample from the ocean. If you’re trying to find out the average composition of the ocean’s water, you’d want to study as big a scoop as possible.”

articles.full_text:
Alissa Totman ’13 was a sophomore when she joined MIT BrainTrust, a student-run organization that connects Institute undergraduates and people with brain injuries for support and socializing. “That group was a great way to learn about the human experience of what people go through when they experience a brain injury,” she says. And it laid the foundation for her life’s work.



Today, Totman is a physician specializing in brain injury medicine at the University of Pittsburgh Medical Center, where she treats adults with head trauma, stroke, brain tumors, and more. 



She is also the founder of Synapse, a nonprofit focused on providing support for such individuals. The organization grew out of a group she started with Jaclyn Konopka ’14 during medical school at Stanford, and Totman launched it as a national service organization in 2016, while pursuing her master’s degree in public health at Harvard. 



There are now chapters at 28 universities across the country—and Totman still runs the organization. “There’s a big need for more resources like this,” she says.

Tomás Villalón Jr. ’14 was raised in San Antonio, Texas, but vividly remembers smog hanging over the city his family came from—Monterrey, Mexico, a steel manufacturing and metal fabrication hub. Even as a child, he realized it was problematic to breathe that air. 



“I’m motivated because I’ve seen what metal-making does,” says Villalón, who majored in materials science and engineering. He started thinking about sustainable metallurgy senior year while working at Boston Metal, an MIT spinoff focused on decarbonizing steelmaking. In 2019 he cofounded Phoenix Tailings, which has developed an efficient process for extracting rare earth metals from mining waste.









“The mining ecosystem by itself makes over several billion tons of waste,” says Villalón, who serves as chief technology officer. (Others on the founding team are Michelle Chao ’17, Nick Myers, and Anthony Balladon.) “We have to get rid of this pollution.”



The company asserts that its proprietary electrochemical technique for processing rare earths generates no toxins and is carbon-free when fueled by renewables.

articles.title: The Internet goes on high alert after discovery of 8 compromised TLS certs
articles.summary: Intermediate certs allow anyone to mint web credentials for any Internet server.
articles.full_text:
Security personnel around the world are on high alert Tuesday following the discovery of eight TLS certificates with private keys so weak they could allow anyone to mint trusted browser and app credentials for any site on the Internet.
As of late morning Tuesday, browser makers and some major apps and programming languages had blocked all eight of the intermediate certificates. There are no reports of certificate transparency logs, which track the issuance of all browser-trusted certificates, showing the compromised keys being used maliciously. The threat remains far from over, however, because it will be hard and time-consuming to update other key parts of the Internet, such as Linux distributions and embedded and Internet of Things devices.
One word: bonkers
The eight intermediate certificates belong to India-based certificate authority eMudhra Limited. An informal advisory published to emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com over on Tuesday posted the message “We have a problem here - Wayne.” The words were digitally signed using the private key of one of the eMudhra certificates. With proof that the reporting party had control of the key, defenders scrambled because the same key could be used to sign unauthorized certificates that would be trusted by millions of servers worldwide.Read full article

articles.title: Quantum error correction goes well beyond breakeven
articles.summary: A demo of error-corrected qubits shows big reductions in errors as they grow.
articles.full_text:
Running complicated algorithms on quantum computing hardware is going to require the use of logical qubits, where collections of hardware qubits are linked together in ways that allow errors to be detected and corrected. In general, the more hardware qubits you dedicate to each logical qubit, the better the chances are of identifying errors. But, given that the hardware qubits are prone to errors, adding more of them also increases the probability that errors will occur. If the hardware error rate is too high, then growing the logical qubit will only make matters worse.
Fortunately, several companies have demonstrated hardware where the error rate is not too high. Several demonstrations show logical qubits are beyond the breakeven point, where adding more qubits improves performance. The problem is that the improvement isn't very dramatic. To lower error rates to levels we'll need to run complex algorithms, we'd have to add a completely impractical number of qubits to each logical qubit.
On Monday, Quantinuum announced that its current generation of hardware is capable of scaling well beyond the breakeven point. Each step up in the size of logical qubits improved some measures of their performance by a factor of over 10.Read full article

The human desire to go fast is old, dating back at least as far as the first time some adventurous Yamnaya saw a horse on the Pontic-Caspian steppe and thought, “I bet if I jumped on that thing’s back, it would be faster than walking.”
A thousand years later, someone else invented the wheel—and the chariot—and humanity was ready to roll. Now, about five millennia since that first horseback ride, equestrianism is mostly a leisure activity, and we drive cars, propelled by motors with more power than an entire herd of beasts could muster.
Acceleration, top speed, and lap times are the usual ways we quantify that performance, and performance electric vehicles are currently in an arms race to see which one can hit 60 mph in the least amount of time. But measuring a car’s performance is easy—all you need is a stopwatch and a track. How about measuring the effect of car performance on the driver? articles.title: Meta Muse exposes users' personal and business secrets when they share conversations
articles.summary: Meta is suspending the sharing feature while it investigates its privacy.
articles.full_text:
Muse, the new general-purpose AI agent from Meta, can expose sensitive information when users share conversations through web links, researchers reported Monday. In response to questions from Ars about the behavior, Meta said it's suspending the sharing feature while the company reviews it and considers making changes.
Like many online services, Muse has allowed users to share searches, conversations, images, and similar content with other people. Such share features usually involve clicking an option to create a unique URL that anyone can use to load a page hosting the content. To keep potentially sensitive information from being accessible to unintended people, the URLs typically contain a long sequence of text that can’t be easily guessed.
A single query is all that's required
Muse, which Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said last month was “built from the ground up for privacy and security,” seems to take the same precautions. But a central design decision for constructing URLs has made the links easy to discover. As a result, researchers from security firm Claroc said they were able to enumerate 6,800 links Muse users created for sharing conversations with others. As I sat in the cab of the pickup truck and manually rolled down the windows, I closed my eyes and, for the briefest moment, flashed back to opening the windows on a cold, winter day in my dad’s 1975 Ford Ranger to let more cigarette smoke escape. I opened my eyes and looked through the windshield at a wall in the Slate Customer Experience Center studded with bright color chips.
Last week, in a former Tesla store staffed by some former Tesla employees, Slate opened its first showroom. Located in the Fulton Market District just northwest of the Chicago Loop, the Slate Experience Center is a place for would-be buyers to poke around a prototype, check out customization options, buy some Slate merch, and even preorder a new Slate Truck with a $300 deposit.
Designed for the American obsession with pickup trucks, the Slate Truck is a bare-bones electric pickup truck retailing for $24,950. It sports plastic panels, a minimalist interior design sensibility, actual window winders, and a projected range of 205 miles. Japan launched a $578 million mission Monday on a five-year expedition to land on the largest moon of Mars and retrieve samples for return to Earth, a daring international project that could yield new insights into the formation of the Solar System.
The robotic Martian Moons eXploration mission, known as MMX, lifted off at 3:41 pm EDT Monday (4:41 am Japan Standard Time Tuesday) from Tanegashima Space Center in southern Japan.
The MMX spacecraft rode into orbit atop a 207-foot-tall (63-meter) H3 rocket, Japan's flagship launch vehicle. My latest vibe coded game experiment is a Command & Conquer style RTS (Real Time Strategy) game called Battle Drones (play it here). Unlike my previous experiments, this one is actually fun to play. I'm somewhat embarrassed to admit that I got there by telling Claude to "Make it a LOT more fun". It also supports multiplayer between nearby devices using audio to synchronize game state! Here's what I've built so far, and some of the things I learned along the way.


  Battle Drones
  How I built this
  v1: the initial prototype
  v2: full sprites
  v3: varied terrain
  v4: the fun update
  v5: Battle Drones goes 3D
  v8: Archipelago
  v10: Goliath, and agent battles
  Agent battles
  v11: Random Maps
  v12: Multiplayer via sound
  Some thoughts
  Update: Online multiplayer support


Battle Drones
My initial goal was to build an RTS game I could play on my phone, in the style of Command & Conquer. I have fond memories of the 1995 original (I liked Red Alert too) and wanted to recapture a little bit of the magic.
After 12 major iterations (and 321 commits by coding agents, mainly Claude Code) I now have a browser-based game that works on mobile and desktop, has multiple play modes, several maps (including a random map generator) and even supports multiplayer for two devices within microphone range of each other. (Update: also online multiplayer; the audio multiplayer induced headaches!)
Here's a video demo of Battle Drones running in a desktop browser:

 

Features so far include:

9 buildings, 7 ground vehicles, 6 aerial vehicles, 3 infantry units - all 3D models, which you can browse here

Fog of war
Different weapons are needed to target aerial or ground vehicles

Six maps, across five biomes - temperate, desert, arctic, volcanic, tropical
A random map generator

Skirmish mode - red vs. blue on a rotationally symmetrical map

Last Stand mode - one player holds out against as many waves of enemies as possible
Area effect weapons: Barrage, EMP, Drop Pod, Sky Hammer

Crate drops with bonus resources
In-game music that responds to events - it gets more intense as fighting breaks out
Different in-game AI personalities (Balanced, Rush, Air Swarm, Boom, Skyforce, Ironclad)

AI vs. AI mode, to watch those personalities play each other
The Goliath - a giant stomping mech with laser eyes and arm cannons and the ability to establish a new base

Mutators that add extra rules or twists
A "Daily Op" challenge
Ranks and achievements (Medals)

Agent vs. Agent mode where two LLMs can play Battle Drones against each other
A multiplayer mode based on two nearby phones communicating via audio messages, an extension of my earlier experiment with Chirp Pong


How I built this
Battle Drones is heavily vibe coded - I've reviewed almost none of the code, and it's built in a language (TypeScript) that I've hardly used myself. I've playtested it quite a bit though, and it's been through a large number of iterations since I started the project.
Here's a rough history of the project so far, including key prompts and links to transcripts.
v1: the initial prototype
I started out with Claude Fable 5 back in July:

We are going to build a mobile friendly RTS game - command and conquer style - called Battle Drones, in which two armies of drones (both flying and ground-based) battle for territory and resources
Let's start with a MVP design, ask me some questions

Here's a shared transcript. I'd given Claude Code for Web an environment variable with an OpenAI API key and told it to use the OpenAI Image Generation API for assets, which got me some basic sprites.
You can try v1 here - it looked like this:

It's recognizable as an RTS, has building mechanics and the ability to select and direct units, and a basic AI to play against.

This first version was barely a proof of concept, and it wasn't any fun to play.
Claude used the Phaser 2D game framework for these early versions. I didn't even realize this until several iterations later!
v2: full sprites
The second version (try v2 here) added sprites for all of the vehicles and the "AI vs. AI" mode, so I could watch the game playing without having to directly control it myself.
Claude proved reasonably competent at prompting OpenAI's image models to generate sprites. You can browse the v2 sprites in the public/assets/sprites folder.

v3: varied terrain
It still wasn't much fun, and the graphics were boring. It was now October, and I had upgraded to Claude Opus 5.5. I told it:

Massively improve this game. Make the graphics and gameplay better (keep it mobile friendly). Render new graphics using the latest OpenAI GPT image API (lookup details) with the API key in the environment variable. Add new unit types and balance the gameplay better. Also add new buildings and better, more varied terrain.

This resulted in five new maps with generated background tiles in a variety of styles, visible here. Opus also regenerated the sprites, making them much more visually appealing. You can try v3 here - it looks like this:

This is starting to feel like a real game! It still wasn't very fun to play though - I found myself getting bored pretty quickly.
v4: the fun update
So far my Battle Drones experiment was confirming my previous belief that coding agents can build a thing that looks like a game but can't actually make something that's genuinely compelling to play.
I shared this theory with someone over dinner, and then thought to myself that I should give the models a proper chance to prove me wrong. I prompted Opus 5.5 on my phone:

This game isn't fun enough yet. Make it a LOT more fun.

This time I was running in Ultracode mode, where Claude Code (in this case Claude Code for Web) runs "dynamic workflows", described in their docs as:

A dynamic workflow is a JavaScript script that orchestrates many subagents at once.

This kicked off many hours of work. I started it in the evening and didn't get a playable result back until late into the next morning. But the results were spectacular.
You can try v4 here - it looks like this:

I had Claude write its own release notes - here are the highlights:

Every skirmish and Daily Op now opens with a choice, gives the side that's losing a way back, and pulls the armies into the middle of the map. There are also two new ways to play.


Openers: pick Blitz, Industry or Air Wing before the clock starts.

Call-down powers: Barrage, EMP, Drop Pod and the Sky Hammer orbital strike.

Objectives and salvage: Uplink relays, supply drops and wrecks worth scrap.

Feel: combat juice, adaptive music, unit voices and an announcer.

Command: battle alerts, game speed, saved squads and touch placement.

New modes: Last Stand survival waves and an 8-mission Ops campaign.

Progression: heroes, an after-action report with awards, a career, 7 mutators and a Daily Op.

Fights run longer and swing more. In 1,200 AI-vs-AI test matches on Normal, games still undecided after 25 minutes fell from 14% to 0.9%. The share of wins by a side that had been 800+ scrap behind rose from 24% to 46%.

Part of the reason Claude took so long was that it ran over a thousand simulated playtest sessions, and used the results to rebalance the existing units, add new ones, and introduce new features.
v5: Battle Drones goes 3D
After the success of Ultracode at "Make it a LOT more fun", I decided to be more ambitious:

Port this game to three.js with 3D models for all of the buildings and vehicles and landscapes

That was another overnight run. I woke up to this v5 version:

The new 3D models were entirely constructed by Claude in TypeScript code.
v6 (play v6 here) added some more visual polish. v7 (play v7) added robot infantry (troopers, rocket squads, snipers) and a "Condor" troop carrying aircraft.
v8: Archipelago
I was beginning to feel guilty at how little actual design input I had into the game - it really had been a case of me saying "make it more fun" and "add visual polish" for the past few releases.
I'd noticed that the AI didn't use the new infantry and troop carrying aircraft from v7 very often - there wasn't a great strategic reason to use them.
It would be neat if we had a new map with a new game mechanic that actively encouraged players to load up Condors with infantry robots and send them out into the map.
This resulted in my longest prompt yet:

Design a new map. Goal is to make different strategic incentives that encourage use of Infantry and Condors and aerial vehicles.
To do this the map will have limited harvester resources but several more uplinks - but uplinks will be on islands that are inaccessible by land vehicles or infantry. These uplinks can also not be claimed using air vehicles. The ONLY way to get them is to fly infantry there in a Condor.
Armies always start with a Condor and a single squad. If an army has no Condor a new one will be provided for free, flying in from the edge closest to their HQ and landing there. That free condor will come with a single free squad on board.
The two HQs should be entirely separated by water, but still accessible by vehicles thanks to two bridges across the map in different places
I want to encourage a battle over uplinks.
The map should be the times the size of other maps - still square
First research and then critique this design. Only build after we have agreed on any modifications
You get to design a new biome for this

The result was the tropical Archipelago map, with seven island uplinks that players can only capture by flying out infantry in a Condor. It's definitely the most fun map to play, once you've got the hang of the basic game mechanics from the simpler maps. The v9 edition made that map a little more interesting - it now looks like this:

v10: Goliath, and agent battles
I decided to add giant robot mechs to the game - think Jaegers from Pacific Rim, or Titans from Warhammer 40,000.
Here are some of the prompts I used to brainstorm with Claude:

Help me brainstorm ideas for adding giant robots to this game - think dreadnought

articles.title: Nature’s job-satisfaction survey highlights the changing geography of science
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 20 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03327-1A higher proportion of scientists in China and India report feeling optimistic about the future than in the United States and several European countries.
articles.full_text:
Since 2010, Nature has periodically performed a survey on how researchers around the world perceive their careers. The survey asks whether scientists are satisfied in their jobs and optimistic about the future, and the reasons for their responses. The results of the latest survey of nearly 4,000 scientists — published on 13 October — include some surprises (Nature 658, 825–829; 2026), especially in light of the results obtained in the 2018 and 2021 surveys.
What’s the secret sauce for happy scientists at work? These eight countries offer some clues
Respondents in several leading research-intensive nations, including the United States, Germany and the United Kingdom, provided less optimistic answers about the future of their careers when compared with those asked in previous years, according to the survey, which ran in May and June. And a greater share of this year’s respondents think that their career prospects are worse than those of previous generations were. In 2018 and 2021 — during the COVID-19 pandemic — higher proportions of scientists in these countries responded positively to these questions.
By contrast, respondents are less pessimistic in middle-income countries — notably in China and India, which are becoming attractive destinations for researchers. In this year’s survey, 70% of respondents in India feel optimistic about their prospects. Although the share of respondents in China who feel positive about the future (55%) is close to the global average (52%), it is noticeably higher than those of Germany (38%), the United Kingdom (33%) and the United States (34%). There is, however, one caveat: the responses from India’s scientists pre-date the nationwide student protests in July.
Under pressure
It’s hardly a secret that a fair number of high-income nations are going through upheavals that recent generations have not experienced. The US government is slashing funding for some grant programmes and directing money towards its priorities, creating anxiety and uncertainty about the future of some projects and research areas.
China’s AI research is booming: what it’s like to be on the front line
Scientists in Europe might also be looking at large changes to their grants. European nations are devoting a greater share of public funding to defence, which has led to cuts to other budgets, including science. Several universities are being urged to work on defence research.
When it comes to job satisfaction, however, the results are reversed. Survey respondents in India and China have relatively low levels of job satisfaction compared with those in several high-income countries. Only 51% of China’s scientists reported being satisfied and 59% of India’s. By contrast, 65% of respondents in the United States, 67% in Germany and 63% in United Kingdom are satisfied with their jobs. Scientists in Canada had the highest job satisfaction of the surveyed countries: 70% of respondents there were happy with their work.
Rising numbers of Asian and African PhD students choose to study in China
Some low- and middle-income countries are struggling to improve working conditions for their researchers. For instance, scientists in China note that they are under pressure to publish in journals, as we reported in a News feature on artificial-intelligence research in the country (Nature 658, 598–600; 2026). By contrast, scientists in Europe and the United States generally work in environments in which they have higher levels of independence — a strong predictor of satisfaction — than do researchers in low- and middle-income countries.
So what of the future? With US midterm elections next month and various national elections due to follow in the next few years, global politics will probably have shifted again before Nature runs its next career-satisfaction survey — and so will the research landscape.
One thing can be said with high confidence: the next survey’s findings will be different from the 2026 results in ways that we cannot predict.

articles.title: Will this sleep-disorder drug be the next big blockbuster?
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 20 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03310-wOrexin agonists have been approved for the treatment of a type of narcolepsy, yet they could also treat conditions across the health spectrum.
articles.full_text:
When US regulators approved a treatment for narcolepsy in August, some researchers immediately predicted a bright future for the class of compounds it belongs to, known as orexin agonists. Much like blockbuster GLP-1 drugs, such as Ozempic, which were initially approved to treat diabetes but have since taken off as treatments for other conditions, these new drugs seem capable of much more than treating sleep disorders.
First-of-its-kind narcolepsy drug opens door to new therapies for the brain
“Diabetes was the tip of the iceberg for GLP-1s, and I’m convinced the same story will play out for orexin,” says Andrew Plump, president of research and development at Takeda, the Tokyo-based pharmaceutical company that developed the newly approved drug, called Orzeyful (oveporexton). “Our goal now is to unravel the science and understand what’s below the surface.”
This excitement comes on the heels of decades of research about orexins — peptides that are produced by the brain and that have a role in modulating metabolism, mood, appetite, memory and, most notably, sleep and wakefulness cycles. Now, scientists are racing to work out how best to apply what they have found in the clinic, exploring the use of orexin agonists in the treatment of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and other conditions in which attention and alertness are dysregulated.
“Anyone who has gotten a poor night of sleep can tell you that it impacts nearly every aspect of their life,” says Luis de Lecea, a psychiatrist at Stanford University in California, who was among the first to identify orexins. “It is very rewarding to have a hand in something that has led to a drug that helps people.”
Dual discoveries
De Lecea was a budding scientist with a new laboratory at the Scripps Research Institute in San Diego, California, when, in the mid-1990s, he took on a daunting project: identifying proteins produced only in certain parts of the human brain. Groups at the institute were divvying up brain regions to study, and de Lecea chose the hypothalamus, an almond-sized region deep in the brain’s interior.
The team generated a list of hypothalamus-specific messenger RNAs — small chunks of genetic material that carry the instructions for making proteins. Sifting through the list, the scientists identified a pair of neuropeptides that they named hypocretin 1 and 21. Unbeknown to de Lecea, researchers in Texas had, around the same time, isolated the equivalent peptides in rats, dubbing them orexin A and B2.
Neuroscientist Takeshi Sakurai was working in the lab of Masashi Yanagisawa, a molecular biologist then at the University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center in Dallas, when the group first identified the orexins. The researchers suspected that the peptides regulated feeding in rodents — the name comes from the Greek word orexis, meaning appetite — but when they artificially blocked orexin signalling, they found something unexpected.
Narcolepsy confirmed as autoimmune disease
“The animals sometimes abruptly collapsed,” says Sakurai, now at the University of Tsukuba in Japan. The behaviour bore a striking resemblance to a hallmark of narcolepsy type 1 in humans: a sudden, temporary loss of muscle control known as cataplexy. After further work, the team landed on a more complete understanding of the role of orexins. “Orexin does not simply wake us up, it keeps wakefulness stable,” he says.
Back in California, researchers were making more discoveries. Emmanuel Mignot, a sleep-medicine specialist at Stanford, and his colleagues were the first to identify a mutation in the gene that encodes orexin receptor 2 as the cause of canine narcolepsy3. In a study of people with narcolepsy type 1 who had died, Jerome Siegel, a neuroscientist at the University of California, Los Angeles, and his colleagues found that the brains of these people nearly always had a massive loss of the neurons that produce orexins4.
It’s a small population — just 70,000 cells among the hundreds of thousands in the hypothalamus — yet they seem to be crucial.
“Once those neurons are gone, the brain isn’t able to find a workaround,” Siegel says.
Turning knowledge into a drug
From the moment they first noted the link between orexins and sleep, Sakurai says he and his team recognized the therapeutic potential. In a few years, so did pharmaceutical companies.
The first investigations at Takeda began in the late 2000s as a pet project. One of the technicians there had a friend with narcolepsy type 1, and he began looking for a molecule that could bind to orexin receptors and restore a normal sleep–wake cycle.
When the technician scanned Takeda’s libraries for a molecule that met the criteria, only a single candidate, called TAK-925, came back. Going forward with it would be a risk, says Plump. “No chemist in their right mind would start a drug-discovery programme with a single hit.”
First orexin agonists address root cause of narcolepsy
Nevertheless, Takeda researchers gave it a try and the molecule performed well in animals. When the company launched the first human trial in 2017, the technician drove his friend to the study centre so that she could participate. He contacted Plump right away, saying that the drug seemed to work for her. “He could tell just from speaking with her,” Plump says.
Orzeyful, which has now received approval in three countries, builds on the foundation that TAK-925 and other early candidates set. The drug is a marked improvement on existing therapies that only mask symptoms of the disease and often come with severe side effects.
Mignot, who led Takeda’s late-stage trials says that people report that “after they take this drug, suddenly they really know what it is to be awake”.
The next GLP-1?
With the approval of Orzeyful, competitors are now racing to tap into a global market for narcolepsy drugs that analysts predict could top US$6.4 billion by 2031. Narcolepsy — both type 1 and type 2, which is not associated with a die-off of orexin-producing neurons — affects roughly three million people worldwide, and estimates suggest that many more cases go unreported or misdiagnosed.

articles.title: Can a human survive in a whale’s belly? The science behind the thriller Whalefall
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 20 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03358-8Nature spoke to marine and anatomy specialists about the ‘modern-day Jonah’ film. Warning: spoilers ahead.
articles.full_text:

Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles

The new film Whalefall, released on 16 October, takes viewers into the belly of the beast — quite literally. The survival thriller, based on Daniel Kraus’s 2023 novel, follows university student Jay Gardiner (played by Austin Abrams) as he is accidentally swallowed by a sperm whale while scuba diving. Viewers watch with apprehension as Jay treks through the whale’s multi-chambered stomach, looking desperately for a way out — all while reckoning with the anniversary of his father’s death.
The making of both the novel and its subsequent film relied heavily on collaboration with scientific advisors. One of them — Joy Reidenberg, a comparative anatomist at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai in New York City — says she and the storytellers discussed everything from what whale species would work best for the “modern-day Jonah” story to what damage Jay might incur while inside various stomach chambers.
Here, Nature speaks to Reidenberg and Ilias Foskolos, who researches deep-diving toothed whales at both Aarhus University in Denmark and Stanford University in California, to help separate science from fiction.
Jay dives offshore in California and gets mixed up with a giant squid and accidentally swallowed. Is that possible for a sperm whale?
Foskolos: There are a few problems with this. Sperm whales are usually not in coastal areas. They’re oceanic predators. They won’t feed on something that is at shallow depths. Most evidence from sperm whale stomach contents suggests that they consume quite small prey. They consume mostly squid of about 30 to 40 centimetres long — so nothing even close to a person’s size. Sometimes they go for bigger squid, but that’s not very common.
Reidenberg: Sperm whales don’t have much of a mouth to carry anything. But the throat passageway is actually quite large. And if it’s a very large sperm whale, which is the premise for this movie and for the book, then it’s physically possible. Behaviourally, could this ever happen?
You have to realize that the premise of the whole thing is that this sperm whale is pulling [Jay] in accidentally [with a squid]. If you were eating a gummy bear, and someone put a pebble next to it and you put the pebble in your mouth with the gummy bear, you'd probably spit everything back out again because that’s not really what you want to eat. So how likely is it for a sperm whale to ingest a human? About as likely as you are to ingest a rock.
Could a human survive inside a whale’s stomach chambers?
Reidenberg: I think so, if they had enough of the right protection.
The first chamber is supposed to be a mechanical mushing chamber. What that stomach is trying to do is break [Jay] into smaller digestible units. If you’ve got something that’s punching the walls against the person, or constricting like a boa constrictor might around someone’s chest, would it stop that person’s heart? Usually, these muscles are trying to mash up something that doesn't have bones. Humans have bones. So now we’re dealing with a form of resistance that this whale’s not used to encountering. And then add the scuba tank, which is pretty incompressible. It’d be pretty unlikely that the stomach would constrict all of the chest, because you still have that area where the ribs meet the tank.
If the scuba diver has a dry suit on, then stomach acids [in the second chamber] are unlikely to get into that dry suit. Only the areas that are exposed are the areas that would start to burn. And you don’t necessarily die from burns, but that would not be a pleasant experience.
What does the term ‘whale fall’ mean to scientists?
Foskolos: What we call whale fall is just the remains of a dead whale along the sea bottom, which creates entire ecosystems, because they can at times fuel different communities of animals depending on the state of decomposition of the whale, which is amazing.
Reidenberg: There isn’t anything else really growing down there that can provide nutrients. There are lots of scavengers around waiting for something. And when a whale fall comes down, it's like manna from heaven. Everything comes from miles around to feed on this carcass, and it develops its own community.

But formal curricula rarely include these skills. Universities invest years in teaching students how to design experiments and analyse data, but leave peer-review training mostly to informal mentorship.
So, how do early-career researchers — especially students and postdocs — learn to develop a critical eye?
Preprints offer a valuable opportunity for trainees to practise reviewing manuscripts outside the formal journal-review process, and several initiatives have been established with this in mind.
PREreview, for example, is a platform on which researchers can openly review and discuss preprints. And Preprint Club, a cross-institutional journal club run by an international group of universities, allows early-career researchers to select manuscripts for discussion so that they can learn from experience alongside their peers, more-senior researchers and faculty mentors.
Inspired by these efforts, we worked with the Bakar ImmunoX Initiative, a research programme at the University of California, San Francisco (UCSF), to launch our own preprint journal club, called ImmunoX Preprint JC, over the 2025–26 academic year.
We think that the journal club’s greatest value is in helping early-career researchers to build confidence and expertise in peer review. As a result, they are included in every level of conversation, from shaping how the club is run and how preprints are scored to leading discussions during journal-club sessions.
We also feel that other institutions could emulate this model, which combines hands-on experience, mentoring and relationship building, to support the development of their own early-career researchers.
Group discussion
Each monthly ImmunoX Preprint JC session follows the steps below. A postdoc starts by selecting an immunology-related preprint posted on the bioRxiv server. They choose an ImmunoX faculty ‘coach’, who helps them to assess the preprint on the basis of its scientific quality, impact and novelty. The manuscript and scoring rubric are shared with the wider ImmunoX community before the meeting.
At the meeting, the postdoc leads a 20-minute presentation discussing the preprint’s strengths and proposing experiments to improve it. Attendees then have a five- to ten-minute discussion about the preprint’s strengths and weaknesses; this is followed by anonymous scoring of the manuscript in terms of its scientific quality, impact and novelty.
Each manuscript’s publication status is tracked over several weeks to assess how well the ImmunoX community evaluated it. We plan to have the presenter of the top-scoring preprint over a six-month period write up a commentary with their coach. The piece would then be shared with the ImmunoX community and general public online.
Tracking progress
A key goal for the ImmunoX Preprint JC is to gauge whether the community-based assessment of a preprint reflects whether it is eventually accepted by a journal. Such data can establish a benchmark for how well our community — especially trainees — evaluates the scientific merits of a preprint.
We consulted with the Immunology Preprint Club at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai in New York City to compare scores given by both groups to the same preprints.
We also compared the preprints’ real-life performance with our scores. Although most of the preprints we have so far reviewed remain unpublished, our top-scoring paper was subsequently published in Cell1 — a leading life-sciences journal — suggesting that community-based assessments can, at least in some cases, identify work that will go on to meet the standards of a high-profile journal. Our findings from the 2025–26 academic year can be viewed in more detail on the ImmunoX website.
Assessing our own data allows us not only to track occasions we’ve correctly identified high-quality work, but also to pick up on potential biases. For example, we noticed that manuscripts whose senior authors were highly cited tended to receive higher scores in our journal-club sessions. This could mean that our community reliably identified rigorous science, or it might reflect an unconscious bias correlating reputation with scientific quality.
Learning to notice this will help trainees to develop more self-awareness, which is crucial for an unbiased peer-review process. In the future, we plan to withhold manuscript author names until the end of a scoring session.

China has selected its first group of young researchers to receive funding for up to 15 years, in one of the longest research grants on offer to scientists globally.
Most research funding is awarded in grants that last for five years or less, says Nicole White, a statistician at Queensland University of Technology in Brisbane, Australia. But short funding cycles favour projects that are able to deliver results quickly, which can disadvantage high-risk but potentially ground-breaking research and cut promising work short before its impact is fully realized, she says. “Some of the most impactful scientific discoveries have taken decades, not years, to achieve,” White adds.
Dou Xiankang, president of the National Natural Science Foundation of China (NSFC), described the agency’s latest initiative at a forum held by the New Cornerstone Science Foundation in Shenzhen on 19 September. He said that 44 researchers under the age of 35 (women under 38) had been chosen, including 9 from outside China, as part of the National Distinguished Young Scientists Fund. Their names and projects have not been released.
At the forum, Dou said the 15-year grants would work in a “five-plus-five-plus-five arrangement”. That means, recipients whose initial five-year grants were about to end could be considered for a second five years and after ten years, another portion would be selected for a third five years of funding.
“During those 15 years, we will not conduct any short-cycle, short-term target assessments. We will assess only one thing: whether you are there in the laboratory,” Dou told the forum.
The NSFC first announced plans to create 15-year grants in 2023, stating that initial 5-year grants would be worth 4 million yuan (US$596,000), they would then double to 8 million yuan for the second 5 years, and then double again to 16 million yuan for the final 5 years.
The NSFC has been ramping up funding for young researchers. Earlier this year, it pledged to increase the number of grants it provides for early-career scientists by 50%, adding 12,000 projects through its Young Scientists Fund.
